Safety cannot be an afterthought, because the hazards are severe and varied. High voltages and currents throughout the equipment can electrocute. Induction coils, though their fields do not burn skin at a distance, can heat any conductor placed in them, so rings, watches, tools and, critically, surgical implants and pacemakers are endangered, and molten metal, red-hot parts and quench media cause burns and steam explosions. Radio-frequency and microwave fields can heat tissue and interfere with electronics, requiring shielding and exposure limits. Arc processes emit intense ultraviolet and visible radiation that damages eyes and skin, and fumes that must be extracted. Consequently these installations depend on interlocked guarding, emergency stops, insulation and grounding, cooling systems, fume extraction, personal protective equipment, and trained operators; the safety note accompanying this guide states the essentials plainly.

Several other misconceptions deserve correction. Induction does not require contact and does not heat by the coil touching the part; the coil stays comparatively cool and heats through its field. Microwaves do not cook from the centre outward in general, but heat wherever the field and absorbing molecules coincide, which is often but not always the interior. Non-conductive, non-magnetic materials cannot be induction-heated directly and need a susceptor. And electric heating is not free of energy accounting merely because there is no visible flame; every watt of heat traces back to generation. Keeping these realities in view lets an engineer choose and run electric heating soberly, exploiting its precision while respecting its costs and dangers.

sections.heading: Where it connects onward: materials, power electronics and decarbonization
sections.body:
Industrial electric heating does not stand alone; it is a junction where several large fields meet, and appreciating those connections turns isolated facts into understanding. It rests first on electromagnetism and physics, the Faraday, Lenz, Joule and Maxwell relations introduced earlier, together with the thermodynamics and heat-transfer principles, conduction, convection and radiation, that govern how deposited energy moves and how much escapes. A reader who grasps skin depth, hysteresis and the Curie point holds the same tools used to understand transformers, motors, electromagnetic shielding and antennas, because all are governed by how alternating fields interact with conductors and magnetic materials.

Its second great connection is to materials science and metallurgy. Heating exists to change materials, so the payoff lies in phase transformations, the austenite-to-martensite transformation exploited in induction hardening, recrystallization and grain growth in annealing, melting and solidification in casting, and diffusion in sintering and heat treatment. Choosing a heating method and recipe is inseparable from knowing the target material's transformation temperatures, thermal conductivity, and response to heating and cooling rates. The purity advantages of vacuum induction, electron-beam and arc remelting connect directly to the demanding requirements of superalloys, titanium and specialty steels for aerospace, energy and medicine.

Third, electric heating is now driven by power electronics, and its recent progress is largely their progress. The insulated-gate bipolar transistors and field-effect transistors that make efficient high-frequency, high-power inverters possible are the same devices that power electric vehicles, renewable-energy inverters and industrial drives. Advances in wide-bandgap semiconductors of silicon carbide and gallium nitride are pushing induction supplies to higher frequencies, powers and efficiencies. Control theory, sensing and increasingly model-based and data-driven optimization refine the heating process, and electromagnetic and thermal simulation has become integral to design.

The fourth and increasingly decisive connection is to energy and the environment, which is why this guide is filed under that heading as well. Much industrial heat has historically come from burning fossil fuels, and industrial heating is a large share of global energy use and carbon emissions. Electrifying heat, replacing gas furnaces with induction, resistance and other electric methods powered by low-carbon electricity, is a central strategy for decarbonizing industry. Electric methods also offer efficiency, flexibility to follow variable renewable supply, and the possibility of pairing with heat pumps, thermal storage and hydrogen where very high temperatures or chemistry demand it. The electric arc furnace's role in recycling steel is already one of the largest concrete contributions to lower-carbon metallurgy.

Finally, the field connects to manufacturing and automation, where electric heating's speed, precision and controllability make it a natural fit for automated, high-throughput, high-quality production, and to the adjacent technologies of welding, cutting, coating and additive manufacturing that increasingly use the same laser, electron-beam and plasma sources. Seen whole, industrial electric heating is a mature yet actively advancing discipline, sitting at the crossroads of physics, materials, electronics and the energy transition, and a reader who follows those threads outward will find the subject opening onto much of modern engineering.

guides.title: Avionics and flight instruments
guides.summary: How aircraft instruments and electronic systems sense the air, the Earth and the radio spectrum to tell a crew where they are, how fast they are going and which way is up. Covers pitot-static and gyroscopic instruments, air data computers, inertial and satellite navigation, radio aids, glass cockpits, autoflight, data buses, redundancy and the characteristic failure modes of each.

sections.heading: What Avionics Means and Why It Matters
sections.body:
Avionics is a compression of "aviation electronics", and in modern usage it covers essentially every electrical
and electronic system on an aircraft that is not there simply to make the engines turn or the lights work:
flight instruments, navigation and communication radios, autopilots, flight management computers, surveillance
equipment, weather radar, recording systems and the data networks that connect them. On a modern airliner
avionics account for a substantial fraction of the aircraft's cost — commonly quoted figures put it above 30
per cent for a commercial transport and considerably higher for a military type — which is a reasonable measure
of how much of the machine is now information handling rather than metal.

The reason the subject exists is a simple and unforgiving fact of human physiology. Human beings cannot
determine their own orientation without visual reference to the horizon. The vestibular system of the inner ear
senses angular acceleration, not angular position, and its sensory threshold means a roll entered at less than
roughly 2 degrees per second is not detected at all. Sustained turns are perceived as level flight within about
20 seconds as the fluid in the semicircular canals catches up with the motion. Consequently a pilot in cloud,
fog or a dark night without instruments will, with near certainty, enter a spiral descent while believing the
aircraft is straight and level. Studies conducted for the United States Federal Aviation Administration in the
1950s put the average survival time for a non-instrument-rated pilot entering cloud at around 178 seconds, and
the number has stayed grimly stable in accident statistics ever since. Instruments are not a convenience; they
substitute for a sense the body does not possess.

The information a crew fundamentally needs divides into a small number of quantities. How fast the aircraft is
moving through the air, which determines whether the wing is producing lift or about to stop doing so. How high
it is, both above the sea and above the ground. Which way it is pointing and which way it is actually going.
What attitude it holds relative to the horizon in pitch and bank. Where it is on the Earth. Where other aircraft
and terrain are. And what the machinery itself is doing.

Each of these is derived from a physical measurement of something else, and every instrument is therefore an
inference. Airspeed is inferred from a pressure difference, altitude from a pressure, attitude from the
behaviour of a spinning mass or a vibrating structure, position from the timing of radio signals. Every
inference has assumptions that can be violated, and almost every serious avionics accident traces back to an
assumption quietly failing while the display continued to look entirely plausible.

sections.heading: The Pitot-Static System: Pressure as the Primary Sensor
sections.body:
Three of the six classic flight instruments — airspeed indicator, altimeter and vertical speed indicator — are
not electrical at all in their simplest form. They are pressure gauges, driven by a plumbing system that samples
two different air pressures and lets the difference and the absolute value do the work. Understanding this
system is the foundation of everything else, because even in a fully digital aircraft the underlying
measurement is unchanged; only the gauge has been replaced by a computer.

The physics is Bernoulli's principle applied to a moving airframe. Air brought to rest at a forward-facing
opening exerts a pressure equal to the ambient static pressure plus the dynamic pressure produced by its motion.
That combined value is called total, ram or pitot pressure. Meanwhile a port flush with the fuselage skin, set
where the airflow is undisturbed and parallel to the surface, samples static pressure alone. The difference
between them is dynamic pressure, given by q = ½ρV², where ρ is air density and V is true airspeed. Solve for V
and you have a speed measurement from nothing but two pressures.

The pitot tube itself is a forward-facing probe, typically mounted on the nose or beneath a wing well clear of
propeller wash and boundary-layer disturbance. Inside, a small chamber connects to the instrument line, and a
drain hole at the bottom lets water escape. Because a blocked pitot tube produces dangerously wrong airspeed,
the probe is electrically heated — typically a few hundred watts per probe — and pitot heat is a checklist item
before entering visible moisture at low temperature. Static ports are usually a pair, one on each side of the
fuselage, cross-connected so that sideslip raising the pressure on one side and lowering it on the other largely
cancels out.

Static system errors matter more than they might appear. Position error arises because no location on an
aircraft samples truly undisturbed pressure at every angle of attack and Mach number; the correction is
established by flight test and either engraved on a placard or applied automatically. An alternate static
source, drawing from inside the cabin, is fitted to most aircraft as a backup. Because cabin pressure in an
unpressurised aeroplane is usually slightly lower than ambient owing to airflow around the fuselage, selecting
alternate static typically makes the altimeter read slightly high and the airspeed slightly fast, and the flight
manual gives the correction.

Maintenance of these systems is tightly regulated for good reason. Certification requires periodic leak checks
of the static system, and a great many fatal accidents have followed from a port blocked by tape after washing,
by insects, or by ice.

sections.heading: The Airspeed Indicator and the Four Airspeeds
sections.body:
The airspeed indicator is mechanically the simplest instrument and conceptually one of the most subtle, because
the number a pilot reads is deliberately not the aircraft's actual speed through the air, and the reasons for
that are sound.

Mechanically, the instrument is a sealed case fed with static pressure, containing a flexible capsule fed with
pitot pressure. As dynamic pressure rises the capsule expands, and a linkage drives the needle. The dial is
calibrated by inverting q = ½ρV² using a fixed value of ρ — the International Standard Atmosphere sea-level
density of 1.225 kilograms per cubic metre. That fixed assumption is what makes the reading indicated airspeed
rather than true airspeed, and it is the source of all the confusion and all the utility.

Four quantities need distinguishing. Indicated airspeed, IAS, is simply what the dial shows. Calibrated
airspeed, CAS, is IAS corrected for instrument and position error, and the two are close in cruise and diverge
at high angles of attack. Equivalent airspeed, EAS, is CAS corrected for the compressibility of air, a
correction negligible below roughly 200 knots and 10,000 feet but significant for fast, high aircraft. True
airspeed, TAS, is EAS corrected for actual air density, and it is the aircraft's real speed relative to the air
mass. A useful rule of thumb is that TAS exceeds IAS by roughly 2 per cent per thousand feet of altitude, so an
aircraft indicating 250 knots at 30,000 feet is genuinely doing about 400 knots. Ground speed is TAS combined
vectorially with the wind, and only satellite or inertial navigation measures it directly.

The crucial insight is that aerodynamics cares about dynamic pressure, not speed. A wing stalls at a particular
angle of attack, and at a given weight and configuration that corresponds to a particular value of q — which
means a particular indicated airspeed, regardless of altitude. The stall speed of a light aircraft shown as 50
knots indicated is 50 knots indicated at sea level and at 12,000 feet, even though the true speed is very
different. This is why every operating speed is quoted in indicated terms and why the instrument is deliberately
left uncorrected.

Dial markings encode the limits directly. The white arc spans the flap operating range, from stall speed with
flaps extended to the maximum flap extension speed. The green arc is the normal operating range. The yellow arc
is a caution range permitted only in smooth air. The red radial line marks never-exceed speed. Additional
markings show best rate-of-climb and best angle speeds on some types, and jets add a barber-pole needle driven
by an air data computer to show the varying maximum operating speed, which becomes Mach-limited with altitude.

sections.heading: The Altimeter and the Problem of Pressure Settings
sections.body:
The pressure altimeter is an aneroid barometer with a scale marked in feet or metres instead of pressure units.
Inside a case vented to static pressure sits a sealed, partially evacuated capsule; as static pressure falls
with height, the capsule expands and a gear train drives the pointers. Because the relationship between
pressure and height is not linear, the gearing is deliberately non-linear, and the instrument's calibration
follows the International Standard Atmosphere: 1013.25 hectopascals and 15 °C at sea level, with temperature
falling at 1.98 °C per thousand feet up to the tropopause at 36,090 feet.

Near sea level, pressure falls by roughly 1 hectopascal per 27 feet, or about 1 inch of mercury per thousand
feet. That gradient makes the instrument sensitive but also creates the central operational problem: real
atmospheric pressure at sea level varies from day to day and place to place, so an uncorrected altimeter would
be wrong by hundreds or thousands of feet. The solution is a subscale, adjusted by a knob, that lets the pilot
enter the current datum pressure. Three settings are used. QNH sets the altimeter to read height above mean sea
level, so it reads airfield elevation on the ground. QFE sets it to read zero on the runway, giving height above
that aerodrome. And the standard setting of 1013.25 hectopascals, used above a defined transition altitude,
gives flight levels — nominal altitudes that guarantee vertical separation between aircraft even when all of
them are wrong by the same amount relative to the sea.

The classic error is captured by the aviator's phrase "from high to low, look out below." Flying from an area of
high pressure into one of low pressure without resetting the subscale leaves the altimeter over-reading, so the
aircraft is genuinely lower than indicated. A 10-hectopascal drop is about 270 feet of unannounced descent.
Temperature produces an analogous and more insidious error, because the instrument assumes standard lapse rate:
in air colder than standard the true height is lower than indicated, by roughly 4 per cent of the height above
the setting datum for each 10 °C below standard. At −30 °C on the surface, an indicated 2,000 feet above the
aerodrome may be barely 1,500 feet, which is why cold-temperature corrections to approach minima are mandatory
in many jurisdictions.

Radio altimeters solve a different problem. They transmit a frequency-modulated signal downward, typically in
the 4.2 to 4.4 gigahertz band, and derive height above terrain from the frequency difference between the
transmitted and received signal. They are accurate to a few feet and are used below about 2,500 feet for
autoland, ground-proximity warning and approach callouts. Their measurement is height above whatever is
directly beneath the aircraft, not above sea level, and the two must never be confused.

sections.heading: The Vertical Speed Indicator
sections.body:
The vertical speed indicator, also called the rate-of-climb indicator or variometer, measures how fast static
pressure is changing and presents that as a rate of climb or descent in feet per minute. It completes the
pitot-static group and is the only one of the three that measures a derivative rather than a value.

The mechanism is a neat piece of pneumatic engineering. A capsule is connected directly to the static line, so
its interior tracks ambient static pressure immediately. The case surrounding it is also connected to the static
line, but through a deliberately restricted orifice called a calibrated leak. In level flight both pressures
equalise and the capsule is undeflected, so the needle reads zero. In a climb, static pressure falls; the
capsule interior follows at once while the case lags behind because air can only bleed out slowly through the
restriction. The resulting differential deflects the capsule, and the deflection is proportional to the rate of
pressure change — which is to say, to vertical speed.

The consequence of that design is lag. The instrument needs perhaps six to nine seconds to settle after a pitch
change, and during the first moments of a control input it can move briefly in the wrong direction, a behaviour
sometimes called reversal error. A pilot who chases the vertical speed needle will therefore oscillate. The
correct technique is to fly attitude and power for the desired performance and use the vertical speed indicator
as confirmation once it has stabilised.

Instantaneous vertical speed indicators, or IVSIs, reduce the lag with a small accelerometer-driven pump — two
spring-loaded pistons, called dashpots, that respond immediately to the vertical acceleration at the onset of a
climb or descent and inject a pressure change into the case before the calibrated leak would have produced one.
This gives an almost immediate indication, at the cost of some susceptibility to spurious readings during
turbulence and steep turns, where vertical accelerations occur without any sustained change of altitude.

In glass cockpits the vertical speed display is usually computed by an air data computer differentiating the
pressure altitude signal digitally, which removes mechanical lag almost entirely and allows a display filtered
to taste. Gliders use an elaborated version, the total energy variometer, plumbed to a special probe so that
the reading is corrected for changes in airspeed. Without that correction, pulling up converts speed into
height and shows a spurious climb; with it, the instrument shows only genuine gains from rising air, which is
exactly what a glider pilot needs to find a thermal. Audio variometers, which turn the same signal into a rising
tone for lift and a falling one for sink, let a glider pilot circle a thermal while keeping their eyes outside
the cockpit — an early and successful example of moving information out of the visual channel because that
channel was saturated.

A practical note: because the instrument depends entirely on the static line, a blocked static port freezes it
at zero regardless of what the aircraft is doing — one of the few conditions in which a perfectly steady
reading is itself the symptom.

sections.heading: Gyroscopic Instruments: Attitude, Heading and Turn
sections.body:
The three instruments that tell a pilot which way is up and which way the aircraft is turning all depend on the
behaviour of a rapidly spinning mass. A gyroscope exhibits two useful properties. Rigidity in space means a
spinning rotor resists any change to the orientation of its spin axis, so a wheel spun up and mounted in
frictionless gimbals holds its direction while the aircraft moves around it. Precession means that a force
applied to the rim produces a reaction 90 degrees onward in the direction of rotation, which sounds like a
curiosity and is in fact the operating principle of the turn indicator and the means by which gyros are erected
and corrected.

Rotors are spun either by air or electrically. In a vacuum-driven system an engine-mounted pump draws air
through the instrument, and a jet directed at buckets on the rotor rim spins it to perhaps 10,000 to 18,000
revolutions per minute. Electric gyros use a small motor and typically run faster. Many aircraft deliberately
mix the two power sources — attitude indicator on vacuum, directional gyro on electric, or the reverse — so
that a single failure cannot remove every attitude reference at once.

The attitude indicator, or artificial horizon, uses a gyro with its spin axis vertical, mounted so the aircraft
can pitch and roll around it. A horizon bar linked to the gimbals stays level with the real horizon while the
symbolic aircraft moves with the airframe. Because bearing friction and aircraft manoeuvres slowly tilt the
rotor, an erection mechanism using pendulous vanes continuously nudges it back to vertical at a rate of a few
degrees per minute — fast enough to correct drift, slow enough to be swamped by short-term accelerations. The
residual errors are predictable: acceleration causes a false climb-and-right-bank indication, deceleration the
opposite, and a rapid 180-degree turn leaves a small residual bank error.

The heading indicator, or directional gyro, uses a horizontally mounted rotor and is not north-seeking at all.
It simply holds whatever direction it is set to, which is why it must be aligned with the magnetic compass in
level unaccelerated flight and re-checked roughly every 15 minutes, since real-world drift of 3 degrees per
quarter hour is typical.

The turn coordinator uses a gyro canted about 30 degrees from horizontal and relies on precession: yaw rate
deflects the display, showing the rate of turn, with a standard-rate mark at 3 degrees per second — a rate that
completes a 360-degree turn in two minutes and is the basis of most instrument procedure timing. Beneath it, an
entirely separate ball in a curved liquid-filled tube — a simple pendulum — shows whether the turn is balanced,
with the ball displaced toward the inside of the turn if there is too little rudder and outward if too much.
The two indications together let a pilot fly a coordinated turn with no external reference at all.

sections.heading: The Magnetic Compass and Its Errors
sections.body:
The magnetic compass is the oldest instrument on the aircraft, the only one that finds north without being told,
and the only heading reference that requires no power at all. For those reasons it remains a required
instrument. It is also, in flight, one of the least trustworthy displays in the cockpit, and a pilot who does
not know its errors will be misled by it.

Construction is straightforward: a float carrying two magnets and a printed card sits in a sealed bowl of a
light petroleum fluid, pivoted so it is free to align with the horizontal component of the Earth's magnetic
field. The fluid damps oscillation and supports the float, reducing pivot friction. The card is read against a
fixed lubber line, and because the card turns while the aircraft turns around it, the numbers run in the
opposite sense to what a novice expects.

Three separate corrections stand between the compass and true north. Variation is the angle between magnetic
and true north at a given place, ranging from a few degrees in much of Europe to very large values near the
poles, and it is printed on charts as isogonic lines. It also changes slowly with time as the magnetic pole
migrates. Deviation is the local error caused by the aircraft's own ferrous metal and electrical currents; it is
minimised by adjusting small compensating magnets during a compass swing and the residual is recorded on a
correction card mounted by the instrument. Turning on a landing light or an alternator can shift deviation
measurably, which is why the card is validated with the electrics in a defined state.

The dynamic errors are the dangerous ones, and both arise because the Earth's field is not horizontal. Except
near the magnetic equator, the field dips into the ground — around 66 degrees at mid latitudes in Europe — and
the vertical component pulls on the card. Northerly turning error, remembered by the mnemonic UNOS (undershoot
north, overshoot south), means that when turning through north the compass initially lags and even indicates a
turn in the opposite direction, while through south it runs ahead. The magnitude at the start of a turn is
roughly equal to the latitude in degrees. Acceleration error, remembered as ANDS (accelerate north, decelerate
south), applies on easterly and westerly headings: accelerating shows a false turn toward north, decelerating a
false turn toward south.

The practical consequence is that the compass is reliable only in straight, level, unaccelerated flight. That
is precisely when the heading indicator should be aligned to it, and why every instrument scan treats the
compass as a slow reference to correct the gyro rather than as a primary display.

sections.heading: Air Data Computers and Attitude-Heading Reference Systems
sections.body:
Modern aircraft replaced the mechanical linkages between sensor and dial with computers, and in doing so
changed what is possible. The sensing physics is unchanged — the same pitot and static pressures, the same need
for an attitude reference — but the outputs became numbers on a data bus that any system can consume.

The air data computer takes pitot pressure, static pressure and total air temperature and computes the whole
family of derived quantities: pressure altitude, baro-corrected altitude, vertical speed, calibrated airspeed,
true airspeed, Mach number, static air temperature and often angle of attack when a vane or differential-pressure
probe is fitted. Pressure is measured by a transducer — historically a vibrating cylinder or quartz resonator
whose frequency shifts with applied pressure, now often a silicon micromachined diaphragm with a piezoresistive
bridge. Because everything downstream depends on these values, transport aircraft carry two or three
independent air data systems with separate probes, and a monitor compares them.

The attitude and heading reference system, or AHRS, replaces the spinning-mass gyros. In place of a rotor it
uses three rate gyroscopes and three accelerometers, plus a magnetometer for heading. Most modern units use
MEMS sensors — microelectromechanical structures etched in silicon, a few millimetres across, in which a tiny
vibrating proof mass experiences a Coriolis force when the device rotates, and that force is read capacitively.
Higher-grade systems use ring laser gyros or fibre-optic gyros, which have no moving parts at all and infer
rotation from the Sagnac effect: light travelling in opposite directions around a closed loop takes different
times when the loop rotates, producing a measurable phase or frequency difference.

Rate sensors alone are not enough, because integrating a rate to get an angle accumulates the sensor's bias
error without limit. An AHRS therefore fuses the sensors: the gyros give excellent short-term response with slow
drift, while the accelerometers give a long-term vertical reference by sensing gravity, and the magnetometer
gives a long-term heading reference. A filter — classically a Kalman filter — blends them by weighting each
according to its estimated uncertainty, trusting the gyros over seconds and the accelerometers over minutes.
This is why an AHRS can be fooled by a prolonged coordinated turn, in which the apparent gravity vector is
tilted, and why good implementations detect sustained turns and inhibit the levelling correction.

The practical gains are large: no vacuum pump to fail silently, seconds rather than minutes to align, no
tumbling in aerobatics, continuous built-in test that can declare its own failure rather than degrading
unannounced, and a single digital output that drives the displays, the autopilot, the terrain warning system
and the flight data recorder alike. The corresponding cost is that a common-mode software fault or a shared
sensor error can propagate everywhere at once, which is why certified installations demand dissimilar
redundancy rather than merely duplicate units.

sections.heading: Inertial Navigation: Dead Reckoning Without the Outside World
sections.body:
An inertial navigation system takes the AHRS idea to its conclusion: if you know your starting position and can
measure every acceleration you subsequently experience, you can compute where you are without reference to
anything outside the aircraft. It is entirely self-contained, cannot be jammed or spoofed, works at any
latitude and in any weather, and for those reasons remains fitted to airliners and military aircraft despite
satellite navigation being cheaper and more accurate.

The principle is double integration. Three accelerometers measure specific force along three axes; three gyros
track the orientation of those axes. Subtracting the local gravity vector and integrating acceleration once
gives velocity, integrating again gives position. Early systems mounted the accelerometers on a physical gimbal
platform held level by the gyros. Modern strapdown systems bolt the sensors rigidly to the airframe and perform
the rotation mathematically, which is only practical because computing became cheap; a strapdown system must
update its attitude solution hundreds of times a second to keep up with the aircraft's motion.

Alignment before flight is essential and takes time. The system must learn its initial attitude and heading, and
it does so by gyrocompassing: sitting still, it senses the Earth's rotation of 15.04 degrees per hour and
resolves the direction of that rotation vector, which points to true north. A full alignment typically takes
five to ten minutes and requires the aircraft not to move, which is why crews are reluctant to be towed
mid-alignment. Latitude must be entered because the horizontal component of Earth rate varies with it, and an
error there produces a heading error.

The unavoidable weakness is drift. Every sensor bias is integrated, so a constant accelerometer bias produces a
position error growing with the square of time, and a gyro bias produces an error growing with the cube.
Navigation-grade systems are specified around 1 to 2 nautical miles per hour of position drift; a ten-hour
flight can therefore end 15 nautical miles adrift, which is unacceptable for a modern approach. There is also a
characteristic 84.4-minute oscillation, the Schuler period, deliberately designed into the system's feedback so
that errors oscillate rather than grow without bound.

The standard remedy is fusion. A modern system blends inertial data with GPS and often DME-DME radio ranging in
a Kalman filter, taking the inertial solution's smoothness and immunity to interference together with the
satellite solution's absolute accuracy. If satellite signals are lost or jammed — an increasingly common
occurrence in some regions of the world — the inertial system coasts with slowly growing error rather than
failing outright, and the crew is given a degrading accuracy figure rather than a blank screen.

Airliners typically carry three such units so that a disagreement can be resolved by majority vote, and the
combined unit is usually called an inertial reference system when it supplies attitude and heading to the
displays as well as position to the navigation computer.

sections.heading: Radio Navigation: Beacons, Bearings and Beams
sections.body:
Before satellites, aircraft navigated by measuring their position relative to ground transmitters, and that
infrastructure is still in place and still used, both as primary navigation in many regions and as the backup
when satellite navigation is unavailable.

The oldest surviving aid is the non-directional beacon, a simple transmitter typically between 190 and 535
kilohertz. The aircraft's automatic direction finder uses a loop and sense antenna to determine which way the
signal arrives, driving a needle that shows relative bearing to the station. It is cheap and needs no line of
sight, but suffers night effect from sky-wave propagation, coastal refraction, and above all thunderstorms,
since the needle points enthusiastically at any nearby lightning discharge.

The VHF omnidirectional range, or VOR, was the backbone of airways navigation from the 1950s and works quite
differently. Operating between 108 and 117.95 megahertz, the station radiates two signals: a reference phase
that is the same in all directions, and a variable phase whose relationship to the reference depends on the
bearing from the station. The receiver measures the phase difference and thereby knows its radial — its magnetic
bearing from the beacon — to an accuracy of about 1 degree. Crucially, the indication is independent of aircraft
heading, which is what makes it easy to fly. Being VHF, it is line-of-sight, so range depends on altitude,
roughly 1.23 times the square root of height in feet, giving about 130 nautical miles at 10,000 feet.

Distance measuring equipment, or DME, supplies range. The aircraft interrogates a ground transponder in the 960
to 1215 megahertz band; the station replies after a fixed 50-microsecond delay, and the aircraft times the round
trip. Because it measures the direct line, it gives slant range, which exceeds ground distance noticeably when
close and high — overhead a station at 6,000 feet the DME reads about 1 nautical mile, not zero.

The instrument landing system provides precision guidance to a runway. A localiser transmitter beyond the far
end radiates two overlapping lobes modulated at 90 and 150 hertz; equal modulation depth means the aircraft is
on the extended centreline, and the difference drives a left-right needle. A glide slope transmitter beside the
touchdown zone does the same vertically, defining a descent path of typically 3 degrees. Marker beacons or DME
give distance. A Category III installation with a suitably equipped aircraft and trained crew supports automatic
landing in visibility measured in a few hundred metres. The localiser needle is deliberately far more sensitive
than a VOR needle — full-scale deflection corresponds to roughly 2.5 degrees rather than 10 — which is why an
approach flown on the localiser demands much finer heading control than an airway.

Two cautions apply. The glide slope radiates false upper lobes at multiples of the true angle, so an aircraft
capturing at 9 degrees follows a path it cannot fly to the ground; the defence is to cross a published fix at
the charted altitude and reject the approach if it does not match. And vehicles inside the sensitive area can
bend the beam, which is why those areas are kept clear in low visibility.

sections.heading: Satellite Navigation and Required Performance
sections.body:
Global navigation satellite systems changed aviation more than any other avionics development of the last forty
years, because for the first time an aircraft could know its position accurately anywhere, without ground
infrastructure beneath it.

The principle is one-way ranging by timing. Each satellite broadcasts a precisely timed signal carrying its own
orbital position. The receiver measures the apparent travel time to each satellite and multiplies by the speed
of light to obtain a pseudorange — "pseudo" because the receiver's own clock is not synchronised to system time,
so every measurement carries the same unknown clock offset. With four satellites the receiver solves four
equations for four unknowns: latitude, longitude, altitude and clock error. That is why four satellites are the
minimum, and why a cheap quartz oscillator suffices in the receiver.

Error sources are well characterised. The ionosphere delays the signal by anything from a few metres to tens of
metres depending on solar activity and elevation angle; the troposphere adds a smaller, more predictable delay;
satellite clock and orbit errors contribute a metre or two; and multipath from reflections adds noise. Geometry
matters as much as ranging accuracy, expressed as dilution of precision — satellites bunched in one part of the
sky give a poor solution however good the individual measurements. A bare receiver typically achieves position
accuracy of around 5 to 10 metres horizontally, with vertical accuracy roughly half as good because all
satellites are above the horizon.

Aviation demands more than accuracy; it demands integrity, meaning timely warning when the solution should not
be trusted. Receiver autonomous integrity monitoring uses redundant satellites to check consistency, needing at
least five to detect a fault and six to identify and exclude it. Satellite-based augmentation systems — WAAS in
North America, EGNOS in Europe, MSAS in Japan — broadcast correction and integrity data from geostationary
satellites, improving accuracy to about 1 to 2 metres and enabling approaches with vertical guidance. Ground-based
augmentation at an airport can support precision approach.

The operational framework built on this is performance-based navigation, in which a route or procedure specifies
required navigation performance — RNP 1, RNP 0.3 and so on — meaning the aircraft must remain within that many
nautical miles of centreline 95 per cent of the time and must alert if containment cannot be assured. The
aircraft's equipment, not a particular beacon on the ground, becomes the qualifying item, which is what allows
curved approaches into terrain that no straight beam could serve and closer route spacing in busy airspace.

Two limitations deserve emphasis. The received signal is extraordinarily weak — around −130 decibel-milliwatts,
below the thermal noise floor, recovered only by correlating against a known code — which makes it trivially
easy to jam with modest power and increasingly practical to spoof with false signals that a receiver cannot
distinguish without additional checks. And the constellations are national infrastructure operated by states,
so aviation deliberately retains inertial and radio alternatives rather than depending on any single system.

sections.heading: Surveillance: Transponders, TCAS and ADS-B
sections.body:
Knowing where you are solves only half the problem. Air traffic control and other aircraft must know it too, and
the systems that achieve this are collectively called surveillance.

Primary radar detects an aircraft by reflecting energy off it and needs no cooperation, but gives no identity or
altitude and struggles with small or distant targets. Secondary surveillance radar solves this by asking. A
ground interrogator transmits on 1030 megahertz and the aircraft's transponder replies on 1090 megahertz. In
Mode A the reply carries a four-digit octal code assigned by the controller — 7700 for a general emergency, 7600
for radio failure, 7500 for unlawful interference, three codes worth memorising. In Mode C the reply carries
pressure altitude in 100-foot increments, always referenced to the standard 1013.25 setting so that all replies
are on a common datum regardless of local pressure.

Mode S added selective interrogation. Each aircraft has a unique 24-bit address assigned by its state of
registry, so an interrogator can address one aircraft rather than shouting at all of them, which drastically
reduces the mutual interference known as FRUIT and garbling that afflicted busy Mode A/C airspace. Mode S also
carries data: aircraft identification, and in enhanced surveillance a set of downlinked parameters including
selected altitude, indicated airspeed, roll angle and track angle rate.

The airborne collision avoidance system, known as TCAS in its widely fitted version, uses the same transponder
signals to build its own picture. It interrogates nearby transponders, tracks their range and altitude, and
computes time to closest point of approach. Around 40 seconds from a projected collision it issues a traffic
advisory — an amber alert to look out. Around 25 seconds it issues a resolution advisory, a commanded vertical
manoeuvre such as climb or descend, and where both aircraft are equipped the two units coordinate over the data
link so that one climbs while the other descends. The Überlingen mid-air collision of 1 July 2002, in which a
controller's instruction contradicted a resolution advisory and one crew followed each, led to the unambiguous
worldwide rule that the resolution advisory is followed even against a controller instruction.

Automatic dependent surveillance broadcast, ADS-B, inverts the model. Rather than being asked, each aircraft
determines its own position from satellite navigation and broadcasts it, typically once per second, on 1090
megahertz extended squitter or on 978 megahertz in the United States. It requires no radar installation, works
over oceans and remote terrain via satellite relay, updates far faster than a radar sweep, and is receivable by
anyone with a cheap software-defined radio — which brings both the public flight-tracking websites and genuine
privacy and spoofing concerns, since the broadcast is unauthenticated and a fabricated target is not difficult
to inject.

The dependence in the name is the key limitation: ADS-B reports whatever position the aircraft's own navigation
system believes, so a faulty or spoofed satellite solution is faithfully transmitted as truth. Ground systems
therefore cross-check against radar or multilateration where available.

sections.heading: The Glass Cockpit: Displays and How They Are Arranged
sections.body:
For most of aviation's history each instrument was a separate mechanism behind a separate dial, and the
arrangement settled into the basic T: attitude indicator top centre, airspeed to its left, altimeter to its
right, heading indicator directly below, with turn coordinator and vertical speed flanking. That layout was
standardised because it matches the eye movements of an efficient instrument scan, and it survives, because
glass displays reproduce it deliberately rather than inventing something new.

A primary flight display consolidates the T onto one screen. The centre is an attitude presentation with a
sky-over-ground horizon, pitch ladder and bank scale. Airspeed appears as a vertical moving tape on the left,
altitude as a tape on the right with vertical speed alongside, and heading as an arc or compass rose at the
bottom. Tapes replaced round dials because they can show trend vectors — a small line predicting where speed
or altitude will be in six or ten seconds — and because operating limits can be drawn directly onto the scale
and moved as weight and configuration change. The flight director, a pair of command bars, shows the attitude
that would satisfy the selected mode, so the pilot flies the bars rather than computing the correction.

The navigation display beside it shows the route, typically in a track-up arc, overlaid with waypoints,
airports, other traffic from the collision avoidance system, terrain shading and weather radar returns. Its
great advantage over a paper chart and a needle is that it shows the aircraft's relationship to the plan
directly, which removes an entire class of mental modelling errors.

Engine and system information moved to a third display: EICAS on Boeing types, ECAM on Airbus. Beyond gauges,
these present the crew alerting function — a prioritised list of faults with, on ECAM, the associated
checklist actions displayed and ticked off as they are completed. Colour is standardised and load-bearing: red
for warnings requiring immediate action, amber for cautions requiring awareness, green for normal, magenta for
selected or commanded values, cyan and white for reference information.

Head-up displays project the same primary symbology onto a combiner glass in the pilot's forward view, focused
at optical infinity so the eye need not refocus between the symbols and the runway. Their real value is the
flight path vector, a small symbol showing where the aircraft is actually going rather than where its nose
points, which lets a pilot fly a precise touchdown point in poor visibility. Enhanced vision systems add an
infrared or millimetre-wave sensor image behind the symbols, and synthetic vision draws a terrain database as
a rendered landscape on the primary display.

Two design lessons are worth stating. First, a display is only as good as its failure annunciation; a screen
showing plausible but wrong data is far more dangerous than a blank one, so comparators flag disagreements
between independent sources and remove misleading data rather than leaving the crew to notice. Second,
integration concentrates risk, which is why standby instruments — an independent attitude, airspeed and
altitude display with its own sensors and battery — remain mandatory even on the most modern aircraft.

sections.heading: Autopilots and Flight Management Systems
sections.body:
An autopilot is a feedback control system, and understanding it as such demystifies most of its behaviour. It
compares a measured state against a commanded one, computes an error, and drives a control surface to reduce
that error. Everything else is refinement.

The simplest useful autopilot is single-axis: a wing leveller that senses roll and drives the ailerons.
Two-axis adds pitch, allowing altitude hold and vertical speed. Three-axis adds yaw damping, which matters on
swept-wing jets because they exhibit Dutch roll, a coupled oscillation in roll and yaw that is uncomfortable
and poorly damped without assistance. Inner loops stabilise attitude at high update rates; outer loops command
attitude to achieve altitude, heading or track. Control law design must respect the aircraft's own dynamics —
a gain high enough to correct quickly can also drive an oscillation — and gains are often scheduled with
airspeed and altitude because the aircraft responds far more sharply at high speed.

Modes are where autopilots confuse crews, and mode confusion is a recognised accident category. A given lateral
mode might be heading select, track, navigation source, localiser capture or approach; a vertical mode might be
vertical speed, flight level change, altitude hold, vertical navigation or glide slope. The crucial discipline
is that the flight mode annunciator on the primary display, not the pilot's expectation, states what the
aircraft is actually doing, and that a commanded value entered in one mode may be ignored in another. A
particularly notorious trap is a vertical speed mode that will happily fly the aircraft to a commanded descent
rate the engines cannot sustain, trading speed for rate until the wing stalls, because the mode's job is to
achieve the rate and nothing else.

The flight management system sits above the autopilot and turns a route into commands. It holds a navigation
database of waypoints, airways, procedures and airport data, updated on the 28-day AIRAC cycle; a performance
database describing the aircraft; and the crew's entered route, weights and cost index. From these it computes
a lateral path and a vertical profile, predicts arrival times and fuel remaining, determines top of climb and
top of descent, and commands the autopilot and autothrottle to fly it.

The system's weakness is that it does exactly what it was told. A mis-entered waypoint, a duplicated identifier
selected wrongly from a list of similarly named beacons, or a wind entry that is badly out will be flown with
complete confidence, which is why independent cross-checking of every entry by the second crew member is
standard practice and why the computed track is compared against the raw navigation display before it is
followed.

Autothrottle or autothrust completes the picture by managing engine power to hold a speed or a thrust setting.
The two philosophies differ meaningfully: Boeing autothrottles physically move the thrust levers so their
position always shows what the engines are doing, while Airbus levers sit in a detent and do not move, with the
commanded thrust shown on the display instead. Neither is wrong, but each demands a different habit of
attention, and pilots transitioning between them are trained explicitly on the difference.

sections.heading: Buses, Power and Redundancy: How Avionics Are Built Not to Fail
sections.body:
What distinguishes certified avionics from ordinary electronics is not cleverness but the discipline applied to
failure. The governing question in every design decision is what happens when this part stops working, and the
answers are written into the architecture.

Communication between units uses standardised buses. ARINC 429, dominant since 1977, is a simple and robust
one-way bus: a single transmitter drives up to twenty receivers over a shielded twisted pair at 12.5 or 100
kilobits per second, sending 32-bit words containing a label, data and parity. Its one-way nature is a safety
feature — a failed receiver cannot corrupt the sender. MIL-STD-1553 uses a command-response scheme with a bus
controller and dual redundant buses. ARINC 664, a profiled version of switched Ethernet used on the A380, A350
and Boeing 787, provides far more bandwidth while guaranteeing determinism through virtual links with
contractually bounded bandwidth and latency, so that traffic cannot interfere unpredictably.

Electrical power is similarly structured. Aircraft power is typically 28 volts direct current on light types
and 115 volts alternating current at 400 hertz on transports, the high frequency chosen because transformers and
motors shrink with frequency, saving considerable weight. Loads are grouped onto buses in priority order, with
essential and emergency buses fed from batteries or a dedicated source so that critical instruments survive a
total generator failure. Large aircraft carry a ram air turbine — a small propeller deployed into the slipstream
— to power flight controls and essential avionics when everything else has failed.

Redundancy takes several forms with different strengths. Duplication catches random hardware failure but not a
design error common to both units. Dissimilar redundancy — different processors running independently written
software to the same specification — addresses systematic error at considerable cost, and is used for flight
control computers. Triplication allows majority voting, so a disagreeing unit can be outvoted rather than
merely detected. Dissimilar sensing matters too, which is why an aircraft may combine barometric altitude,
radio altitude, GPS altitude and inertial altitude.

Software carries its own regime, DO-178C, which assigns a design assurance level from A to E according to the
consequence of failure. Level A software, whose failure would be catastrophic, requires exhaustive requirement
traceability and modified condition/decision coverage testing — meaning every condition in every decision must
be shown to independently affect the outcome — and typically costs several times more per line than ordinary
commercial code. Hardware follows an analogous standard, DO-254.

Environmental qualification under DO-160 explains why avionics look and cost as they do. A box must survive
temperatures from about −55 to +70 °C, rapid decompression, humidity, salt fog, sand, fungus, vibration,
shock, and lightning-induced transients of hundreds of volts on its wiring. It must also neither emit nor be
disturbed by radio-frequency energy, including the high-intensity radiated fields near broadcast transmitters
and radars. These requirements, not the computation involved, are why an aviation display costing thousands of
pounds does a job a consumer tablet appears to do for a fraction of the price — and why a consumer tablet in
the cockpit is legitimate as supplementary information and not as a certified primary instrument.

sections.heading: Diagnosing an Instrument Failure in Flight
sections.body:
The characteristic danger of an instrument failure is not that the display goes blank but that it goes on
showing something believable. A blank screen is an unambiguous problem; a slowly diverging airspeed is a trap,
because the natural response is to trust the instrument and correct the aeroplane, which is exactly wrong.

The accident record makes the point. Aeroperú Flight 603 crashed into the sea in October 1996 after maintenance
tape left over the static ports produced false altitude and airspeed, the crew receiving simultaneous overspeed
and stall warnings at low altitude. Air France Flight 447 was lost in June 2009 after ice crystals briefly
blocked the pitot probes, the autopilot disconnected as designed, and the subsequent manual handling produced a
sustained stall from cruise altitude. In both cases the sensor fault was recoverable; the loss of a coherent
picture was not.

The framework below is for orientation only. The approved flight manual takes precedence.
steps: Fly the aircraft first: set a known pitch attitude and power setting that you have previously verified produces level flight. Attitude plus power gives predictable performance even when every air data instrument is lying.

Identify which instruments disagree and group them by system. Airspeed, altimeter and vertical speed share the pitot-static plumbing; attitude and heading share a power source. A whole group failing points to the common element.

If airspeed alone misbehaves while altimeter and vertical speed look sensible, suspect the pitot side. Blocked at the ram opening with the drain clear, airspeed falls toward zero; blocked at both, it behaves like an altimeter.

If all three are wrong together, suspect the static system. The signature is a frozen vertical speed, an altimeter stuck near the blockage altitude, and an airspeed that under-reads in the climb and over-reads in the descent.

Select the alternate static source if fitted and apply the flight-manual correction. With no alternate in an unpressurised aircraft, the accepted last resort is breaking the vertical speed indicator glass to vent the line to the cabin; that instrument then reads in reverse.
Turn pitot heat on immediately if icing is even possible, and leave it on. A probe that has already blocked may take several minutes to clear.
Cross-check attitude against independent references: the standby instrument, the turn coordinator, the magnetic compass, and any second display driven by a separate AHRS.

If the attitude reference is suspect, fly partial panel — turn coordinator for bank, airspeed and altimeter trend for pitch, small smooth inputs. Large corrections in the wrong reference frame are what cause loss of control.
Disconnect the autopilot and autothrottle if either is fed by a suspect source. Given bad air data they will fly the aircraft into the error with full authority.

Tell air traffic control what has failed and what you need. They can supply ground-derived position, a radar altitude readout, a heading to steer and separation from traffic; asking early costs nothing.
Squawk 7700 if the aircraft's safety is in doubt, and consider diverting somewhere with better weather rather than flying an approach that now depends on the failed system.

sections.heading: Failure Modes, Limits and Honest Uncertainty
sections.body:
Every system described here has a characteristic way of going wrong, and knowing the signature is more useful
than knowing the mechanism in isolation.

Pitot-static faults are the classic killers because the instruments remain plausible. Blockages come from ice,
insects nesting in a probe left uncovered on the ground, and maintenance tape or covers not removed. Static
leaks in a pressurised cabin cause the altimeter to read the cabin altitude rather than the outside, which can
be thousands of feet low. Vacuum-driven gyros fail slowly and silently: the attitude indicator sags over
several minutes, often accompanied by a heading indicator drifting in the same direction, and there is no flag
on many light aircraft installations beyond a small suction gauge that nobody scans.

Electronic systems fail differently. AHRS units can be disturbed by prolonged unusual attitudes or by
magnetometer interference from ferrous cargo or from a phone left on the glareshield. Air data computers can
propagate a single bad sensor to every consumer if the voting logic is inadequate, which is the essence of what
happened with the angle-of-attack input to the Boeing 737 MAX manoeuvring characteristics augmentation system in
the 2018 and 2019 accidents — a design in which one sensor could command repeated nose-down trim. Satellite
navigation fails through jamming, spoofing and, more mundanely, through a navigation database left past its
28-day expiry, which will happily route an aircraft to a waypoint that has been moved or withdrawn.

Display systems introduce their own class of error. A moving map showing the aircraft correctly positioned on a
plan that was itself entered wrongly is completely convincing, and the defence is to cross-check the computed
picture against a raw navigation source — a bearing and distance from a beacon — rather than against another
view of the same computation.

Some genuine uncertainties should be stated plainly. The optimal level of cockpit automation is contested;
there is good evidence that automation reduces workload in cruise and increases it at exactly the wrong moment
during a failure, and the balance between protecting pilots from error and eroding the manual skill needed when
protection is lost remains an open question in human factors research. The rate at which manual flying skill
decays without practice is not precisely known. And the security of unauthenticated broadcast surveillance is
an acknowledged weakness with no agreed solution yet deployed at scale.

The practical conclusions are stable, however. Trust no single sensor. Know which instruments share a common
source and therefore fail together. Keep an independent reference — standby instruments, a handheld receiver,
a portable attitude source — that does not share power, plumbing or software with the primary system. Scan
continuously rather than fixating, since a failure is usually detected as a disagreement rather than as a flag.
And when something is wrong, fly attitude and power first and diagnose second.

guides.safetyNote: This guide explains how flight instruments and avionics work; it is not flight training and confers no authority to operate an aircraft. Diagnosing an instrument failure in flight is a licensed skill practised under instruction, and the correct action always follows the aircraft's approved flight manual and checklists, which override any general description here. Never fly with a known unserviceable required instrument, never dismantle or modify certified avionics or pitot-static plumbing outside an approved maintenance organisation, and treat any suspected static-system or air data fault as a reason to obtain assistance from air traffic control rather than to troubleshoot at low altitude.

guides.title: AC circuit analysis: impedance, phasors and resonance
guides.summary: How alternating-current circuits are analysed: why reactance shifts the timing between voltage and current, how phasors and complex impedance turn calculus into algebra, and how power factor, filters, resonance and the quality factor Q follow from it.
guides.safetyNote: Resonant circuits magnify voltage and current: a series LC fed from a low supply can develop hundreds of volts across the inductor or capacitor, and mains-connected reactive circuits can be lethal even when the source seems harmless. Rate components for the voltage that actually appears across them, discharge capacitors through a resistor before handling, and never assume a de-energised capacitor is safe.

sections.heading: Why Alternating Current Needs Its Own Mathematics
sections.body: Direct-current circuit analysis is disarmingly simple. Ohm's law relates voltage, current and resistance by a single multiplication, resistors in series add, resistors in parallel combine by reciprocals, and Kirchhoff's two laws close the system. Every quantity is a single number. The moment the source starts alternating, that comfortable world breaks, and it breaks because two of the three basic passive components do not respond to voltage at all. A capacitor responds to the rate of change of voltage; an inductor responds to the rate of change of current. Under a steady DC voltage a capacitor eventually carries no current and an inductor behaves like a plain wire, so both effectively vanish from the analysis. Under an alternating voltage neither vanishes, and each introduces something resistors never do: a shift in timing between voltage and current. That timing shift is the whole difficulty and the whole richness. In a resistor, current is largest exactly when voltage is largest; the two waveforms rise and fall together, in phase. In an ideal capacitor the current peaks a quarter of a cycle before the voltage does, because the current is greatest when the voltage is changing fastest, which happens as the voltage passes through zero. In an ideal inductor the reverse holds and the current lags by a quarter cycle. Once voltages and currents around a loop are no longer aligned in time, they can no longer be added as ordinary numbers. Two 10-volt alternating signals in a series loop might sum to 20 volts, or to zero, or to 14.1 volts, depending entirely on their relative timing. Arithmetic that ignores phase gives answers that are not merely imprecise but qualitatively wrong. The payoff for handling this properly is enormous, because almost everything electrical of consequence is alternating. Power grids distribute at 50 or 60 hertz because alternating voltages can be transformed up for efficient long-distance transmission and back down for safe use, a capability direct current lacked entirely until modern power electronics. Audio is alternating current from roughly 20 hertz to 20 kilohertz. Radio is alternating current from tens of kilohertz to tens of gigahertz. Every digital signal, however square it looks on a screen, is a sum of alternating components, and the reason a fast digital edge misbehaves on a long track is entirely an alternating-current phenomenon. The apparatus that tames all of this is a piece of mathematical bookkeeping introduced to engineering by Charles Proteus Steinmetz in 1893: represent each sinusoid by a single complex number carrying its size and its timing, and the differential equations of the circuit collapse into algebra that looks almost exactly like the direct-current algebra it replaced. Resistance generalises to impedance, Ohm's law survives unchanged in form, and the entire toolkit of series and parallel combination, dividers, superposition and Thevenin equivalents carries over intact. That transformation, its consequences for power and filtering, and the spectacular behaviour called resonance that emerges when capacitance and inductance cancel, are the subject here.

sections.heading: The Sinusoid: Amplitude, Frequency, Phase and RMS
sections.body: A sinusoidal voltage is written v(t) = Vp sin(2*pi*f*t + phi), where Vp is the peak amplitude in volts, f is the frequency in hertz, t is time in seconds, and phi is the phase in radians, which fixes where in its cycle the wave sits at t = 0. It is common and convenient to replace 2*pi*f by a single symbol omega, the angular frequency in radians per second, so that v(t) = Vp sin(omega*t + phi). For a 50-hertz mains supply omega is about 314 radians per second; for 60 hertz it is about 377. The sinusoid is not merely one waveform among many; it occupies a privileged position that justifies building an entire analytical framework around it. In any linear, time-invariant circuit, meaning one built from resistors, capacitors and inductors whose values do not change with the signal, a sinusoidal input produces a sinusoidal output at exactly the same frequency. Only the amplitude and the phase change. No other waveform has this property: feed in a square wave and the output is some other shape. Mathematically the sinusoid is the eigenfunction of these systems, and physically this means a linear circuit can be completely characterised by asking, for every frequency, how much does it scale the amplitude and how much does it shift the phase. Because Fourier's theorem, published by Joseph Fourier in 1822, guarantees that any repeating waveform can be written as a sum of sinusoids, understanding a circuit's response to sinusoids means understanding its response to everything. Several different measures of size are in daily use and confusing them causes real errors. Peak value is the maximum excursion from zero. Peak-to-peak is twice that for a symmetric wave, and is what an oscilloscope naturally shows. Root-mean-square, or RMS, is the value that matters for power: it is the DC voltage that would dissipate the same heat in a resistor. For a pure sinusoid the RMS value is the peak divided by the square root of two, about 0.707 of peak. This is why a 230-volt RMS mains supply actually swings to about 325 volts peak and 650 volts peak-to-peak, a fact that determines the voltage rating of every capacitor placed across it. Cheap multimeters measure the average of the rectified waveform and multiply by a fixed factor of about 1.11 that is correct only for a sine; on a distorted waveform such as the current drawn by a switch-mode power supply they can read low by twenty per cent or more, which is why true-RMS meters exist. Phase is measured relative to some chosen reference, most often the source. A phase of positive 90 degrees means a quarter-cycle earlier, a lead; negative 90 degrees means a lag. Since only differences matter, one waveform in any problem may be declared the reference with zero phase, and everything else measured against it.

sections.heading: Where Reactance Comes From: Capacitors and Inductors
sections.body: The opposition a capacitor or inductor presents to alternating current is called reactance, symbol X, measured in ohms like resistance but fundamentally different because it stores energy rather than dissipating it. Both expressions can be derived in a few lines from the defining behaviour of the components, and doing so makes the formulas memorable rather than arbitrary. A capacitor stores charge Q = C*V, so the current, being the rate of flow of charge, is i = C * dv/dt. Apply a voltage v = Vp sin(omega*t). The derivative of sin is cos, multiplied by the inner derivative omega, so i = omega*C*Vp cos(omega*t). Two things fall out immediately. The current amplitude is omega*C*Vp, so the ratio of voltage amplitude to current amplitude is 1/(omega*C), which is the capacitive reactance Xc = 1/(2*pi*f*C). And the current is a cosine where the voltage was a sine, meaning it peaks a quarter of a cycle earlier: the current leads the voltage by 90 degrees. The physical story is straightforward. A capacitor passes current only while its voltage is changing, so the faster the alternation the more current flows for a given voltage, and its opposition falls as frequency rises. At direct current, frequency zero, the reactance is infinite and the capacitor blocks completely. An inductor obeys Faraday's law in the form v = L * di/dt. Apply a current i = Ip sin(omega*t) and the voltage is omega*L*Ip cos(omega*t). The ratio of amplitudes gives the inductive reactance Xl = omega*L = 2*pi*f*L, and now the voltage is the cosine, so the voltage leads the current, or equivalently the current lags by 90 degrees. An inductor opposes change in current, so the faster the alternation the more it resists, and its opposition rises with frequency. At direct current it is a short circuit. Some worked numbers anchor the scale. A 100-nanofarad capacitor at 1 kilohertz has Xc = 1/(2*pi*1000*100e-9), which is about 1592 ohms. At 1 megahertz the same capacitor is about 1.59 ohms, essentially a short circuit, which is why 100 nanofarads is the universal decoupling value beside a logic chip. A useful pair of mnemonics keeps the phase relations straight. For a capacitor, whose symbol is C, the current leads: ICE, meaning I comes before the E of voltage in a C. For an inductor, symbol L, the voltage leads: ELI, meaning E comes before I in an L. Together they form the old workshop phrase ELI the ICE man. The crucial conceptual point is that reactance consumes no average power. Over one quarter cycle the component absorbs energy from the source, storing it in an electric field between capacitor plates or a magnetic field around an inductor's coil, and over the next quarter it returns that energy. The energy sloshes back and forth rather than being converted to heat. Only resistance dissipates, which is why an ideal reactance can carry substantial current while remaining stone cold, and why the current a capacitor draws from the mains is real enough to blow a fuse yet contributes nothing to the electricity bill.

sections.heading: Phasors: Turning Calculus Into Arithmetic
sections.body: Analysing an alternating circuit directly means writing and solving differential equations, since capacitors and inductors are defined by derivatives. For anything beyond a couple of components this becomes miserable. The phasor method eliminates the calculus entirely by exploiting a single identity, Euler's formula, published by Leonhard Euler in 1748: e raised to the power j*theta equals cos(theta) + j*sin(theta), where j is the square root of minus one. Engineers write j rather than the mathematician's i because i already means current. The trick is to regard a real sinusoid as the projection of a rotating complex quantity. Write the voltage as the real part of Vp * e^(j*(omega*t + phi)), which can be split as the real part of [Vp*e^(j*phi)] * e^(j*omega*t). The bracketed part, Vp*e^(j*phi), is a fixed complex number holding the amplitude and the phase and nothing about time. That is the phasor. The remaining factor e^(j*omega*t) is the same for every voltage and current in the circuit, since a linear circuit does not change frequency, so it can be carried along implicitly and dropped from the working. A phasor is usually written in polar shorthand as a magnitude at an angle, for example 10 volts at 30 degrees, or equivalently in rectangular form as 8.66 + j5 volts. The reason this is transformative is what happens to differentiation. Differentiating e^(j*omega*t) with respect to time simply multiplies it by j*omega. So in the phasor domain, the operation of taking a derivative, the thing that made the problem hard, becomes multiplication by the complex number j*omega, and integration becomes division by it. The capacitor relation i = C dv/dt becomes I = j*omega*C*V, and the inductor relation becomes V = j*omega*L*I. Both are now algebraic, and both look like Ohm's law with a complex constant of proportionality. There are two conventions to keep straight. Phasor magnitudes may be expressed as peak values or as RMS values; power engineers almost always use RMS, electronics and communications work often uses peak. Mixing them silently introduces a factor of 1.414 into power calculations. Second, angles may be in degrees for human readability but must be in radians for any actual computation with exponentials. Adding two sinusoids of the same frequency, which is meaningless as ordinary arithmetic, becomes simple complex addition: convert both phasors to rectangular form, add real to real and imaginary to imaginary, convert back. Two 10-volt sources 90 degrees apart give 10 + j10, magnitude 14.14 volts at 45 degrees, which is exactly the answer a careful trigonometric slog would produce after a page of work. The method is bookkeeping, not physics, but it is bookkeeping so effective that it made large-scale alternating-current engineering practical.

sections.heading: Impedance and Admittance: Ohm's Law Restored
sections.body: Impedance, symbol Z and unit ohms, is the complex ratio of the voltage phasor to the current phasor for a component or a network. It is written Z = R + jX, where R is the resistance, the part that dissipates energy, and X is the reactance, the part that stores and returns it. The three elementary components have impedances Z = R for a resistor, Z = 1/(j*omega*C), which equals minus j/(omega*C), for a capacitor, and Z = j*omega*L for an inductor. Capacitive reactance is conventionally negative and inductive reactance positive, which encodes the opposite directions of their phase shifts in a single sign. With this definition, Ohm's law returns intact as V = I*Z, now an equation between complex numbers. The magnitude of Z, computed as the square root of R squared plus X squared, gives the ratio of voltage amplitude to current amplitude. The angle of Z, computed as the arctangent of X divided by R, gives the phase by which the voltage leads the current. A network whose impedance angle is positive is inductive; negative is capacitive; zero is purely resistive. This single complex number therefore carries everything about how the network responds at that one frequency, and the fact that it holds only at one frequency is the essential caveat: impedance is always a function of frequency, and quoting an impedance without a frequency is meaningless. The combination rules are identical in form to the resistive ones, which is the great practical dividend. Impedances in series add directly. Impedances in parallel combine as the reciprocal of the sum of reciprocals, and for exactly two elements the product-over-sum shortcut still works. Because the arithmetic is complex, however, some results are counterintuitive: two impedances in series can have a smaller magnitude than either one alone, if one is inductive and the other capacitive so their reactances partially cancel. A worked example makes it concrete. Take a 1-kilohm resistor in series with a 0.1-microfarad capacitor, driven at 1 kilohertz. The capacitive reactance is 1/(2*pi*1000*1e-7), about 1592 ohms, so Z = 1000 - j1592. The magnitude is the square root of 1000 squared plus 1592 squared, about 1880 ohms, and the angle is the arctangent of minus 1592 over 1000, about minus 57.9 degrees. Driven by 10 volts RMS, the current is 10 divided by 1880, about 5.32 milliamps, and it leads the source voltage by 57.9 degrees. Admittance, symbol Y, is the reciprocal of impedance, measured in siemens, and is written Y = G + jB where G is conductance and B susceptance. It is worth the extra vocabulary because parallel networks add directly in admittance, converting a messy reciprocal calculation into simple addition. Analysts routinely switch between the two representations to keep the arithmetic in whichever form is simpler.

sections.heading: The Whole DC Toolkit, Carried Over Unchanged
sections.body: Perhaps the most valuable consequence of the phasor formulation is not any single formula but the fact that every technique developed for resistive networks continues to work, with complex numbers substituted for real ones. Nothing new has to be learned about circuit topology; only the arithmetic gets harder. Kirchhoff's current law, that the phasor currents entering a node sum to zero, and Kirchhoff's voltage law, that the phasor voltages around a closed loop sum to zero, both hold exactly. They must, because they are statements of charge conservation and energy conservation applied instant by instant, and if a set of time functions sums to zero at every instant then so do the phasors representing them. The voltage divider is unchanged in form: across two series impedances Z1 and Z2, the voltage across Z2 is the source voltage multiplied by Z2 divided by the sum Z1 plus Z2. Now, however, the divider ratio is complex, so it changes both size and timing, and it varies with frequency. That single generalised divider is the mathematical skeleton of every passive filter in existence. Nodal analysis proceeds exactly as before: pick a reference node, write the current law at each remaining node in terms of node voltages and admittances, and solve the resulting simultaneous equations, which are now complex but otherwise ordinary. Mesh analysis with loop currents works identically. Superposition holds, so a network driven by several sources can be analysed one source at a time, provided all share the same frequency; if they do not, each frequency needs its own analysis and the results are combined only at the end in the time domain. Thevenin's and Norton's theorems carry over with complex Thevenin impedances, and they underpin the practically important maximum power transfer condition. For a source of internal impedance Zs = Rs + jXs, maximum power is delivered to a load when the load impedance is the complex conjugate, Zl = Rs - jXs. The reactances cancel and the resistances match. This is why radio engineers speak of conjugate matching and why an antenna tuner exists: its job is to transform a badly mismatched antenna impedance into something the transmitter's output stage sees as its conjugate. It is worth noting that conjugate matching maximises power delivered but caps efficiency at fifty per cent, since as much is dissipated in the source resistance as reaches the load. This is why power distribution deliberately does not match; there the source impedance is kept far below the load, typically by a factor of a hundred or more, to maximise efficiency instead, and the same reasoning explains why an audio amplifier with an output impedance near zero drives an 8-ohm loudspeaker rather than being matched to it. The one genuinely new complication is that impedances are frequency-dependent, so an answer obtained by any of these methods holds only at the frequency assumed. Where a circuit must be understood across a band, the analysis is repeated at enough frequencies to sketch the trend, or, better, kept symbolic in terms of omega so that the whole response falls out as a single expression.

sections.heading: The Series RLC Circuit Worked Through
sections.body: A resistor, inductor and capacitor in series across a sinusoidal source is the standard vehicle for making all of this concrete, and it repays being worked through in full arithmetic at least once. The total impedance is the sum of the three, Z = R + j*omega*L + 1/(j*omega*C), which tidies to Z = R + j(omega*L - 1/(omega*C)). The real part is fixed; the imaginary part is a difference of two frequency-dependent terms, one rising with frequency and one falling. Take R = 50 ohms, L = 10 millihenries and C = 1 microfarad, driven by 10 volts RMS at 1 kilohertz. The inductive reactance is 2*pi*1000*0.01, about 62.8 ohms. The capacitive reactance is 1/(2*pi*1000*1e-6), about 159.2 ohms.
