The rules exist because the failure modes described here kill both the person working and, through a lost neutral or a reversed pump, people who never went near the switchboard.

guides.safetyNote: Three-phase systems operate at voltages and fault energies that kill. Low-voltage three-phase supplies at 400 or 480 volts are lethal on contact and can produce arc flash injuries at a distance; medium- and high-voltage systems can arc across air gaps without contact at all. Variable-speed drives and capacitor banks store lethal charge for many minutes after isolation. Never work on three-phase equipment without proper training, authorisation, safe-isolation procedure, correctly rated test instruments and arc-rated protective equipment. This guide explains how these systems work; it is not an authorisation or a substitute for qualified instruction and the applicable wiring regulations in your jurisdiction.

guides.title: Generators and alternators
guides.summary: How rotating machines turn mechanical power into electricity: Faraday induction, the synchronous alternator and its excitation system, car alternators, DC dynamos, induction generators, voltage and frequency control, paralleling, and the practical business of running, rating and repairing them.
guides.safetyNote: Generator output is live even when the engine is small and the machine looks harmless: a 5 kVA set delivers enough current to kill instantly, and a residual-magnetism field can put voltage on the terminals of a machine that appears switched off. Never connect a portable generator to house wiring without a listed transfer switch or interlock — backfeed energises the utility drop through the transformer at several thousand volts and has killed line workers and neighbours. Run engine-driven sets outdoors only, at least 6 m from any window, door or vent, because carbon monoxide is odourless and a running set in a garage can reach a lethal concentration within minutes. Treat large capacitors, excitation circuits and rotating parts as hazardous until proven dead and stopped.

sections.heading: What a Generator Is and Why Almost All Electricity Comes From One
sections.body:
A generator is a machine that converts mechanical energy into electrical energy. Something turns a shaft, and electric power comes out of terminals. That single trick underpins the overwhelming majority of the world's electricity: coal, gas, nuclear, hydro, geothermal, biomass and wind plants all differ only in what they use to spin the shaft, and every one of them ends in a rotating electrical machine. Only photovoltaic panels, fuel cells and batteries produce electricity without one. Global generating capacity is measured in terawatts, and a single large steam turbine generator in a nuclear station may be rated at 1,000 to 1,700 megavolt-amperes on a shaft turning at 1,500 or 3,000 revolutions per minute. The same physics, scaled down by seven or eight orders of magnitude, runs the alternator charging a car battery and the tiny dynamo on a bicycle wheel.

The terminology is worth settling immediately because it is used loosely. Generator is the general word for any machine producing electricity from mechanical input. Alternator specifically means a generator producing alternating current, which today is very nearly all of them, including the one in a car, whose output is rectified to direct current only after it leaves the windings. Dynamo, in careful usage, means a generator producing direct current directly by means of a mechanical commutator; these were the original electrical machines and are now largely obsolete. Synchronous machine means an alternator whose rotor turns in exact lockstep with the frequency of the electrical output, which is the type used in essentially all power stations and standby sets. Genset or generating set means the whole package of engine plus alternator plus controls.

One deep symmetry is worth grasping at the outset, because it saves a great deal of confusion later. A generator and a motor are the same machine. Drive the shaft and it produces electricity; feed it electricity and it drives the shaft. The distinction is entirely a matter of which way power is flowing, not of construction. A synchronous machine connected to a grid will run as a motor if the prime mover is removed and as a generator if the prime mover pushes harder than the grid resists, and the transition happens smoothly through zero. Railway locomotives and electric vehicles exploit this directly in regenerative braking, running their traction motors as generators to return energy to the supply, and large pumped-storage hydro plants run the same machine as a motor to pump water uphill at night and as a generator to recover the energy at peak demand. Understanding a generator therefore also means understanding a motor, and the reason for treating them separately is convention and the different practical concerns of each role, not different physics. The practical concerns that do differ are worth listing, since they explain almost every design difference you will meet: a generator must hold its output voltage steady as load varies, must share load gracefully with other generators, must survive short-circuit currents several times its rating for a few seconds, and must be driven at a speed its prime mover can actually hold, none of which a motor is asked to do.

sections.heading: Faraday's Law: The Physics That Makes It Work
sections.body:
Everything a generator does rests on one discovery. On 29 August 1831 Michael Faraday, working at the Royal Institution in London, wound two coils on an iron ring and found that switching current in one produced a momentary deflection in a galvanometer attached to the other. Within weeks he had shown that moving a magnet into a coil did the same, and in October he built the first generator, a copper disc spinning between the poles of a magnet with brushes at the axle and rim, which produced a steady current. The principle, now called Faraday's law of induction, is that a changing magnetic flux through a circuit induces an electromotive force in that circuit. Written for a coil of N turns it is e equals minus N times the rate of change of flux, that is e = -N dΦ/dt, where Φ is the magnetic flux in webers and e is the induced voltage.

The minus sign is Lenz's law, stated by Heinrich Lenz in 1834, and it is the single most practically important part of the equation. The induced current flows in the direction that opposes the change producing it. This is why a generator becomes physically harder to turn the more current you draw from it, and why the engine of a genset labours audibly when a large load switches on. Without it, energy would not be conserved and you could get electricity for nothing. The mechanical torque you must supply against that opposition, multiplied by the shaft speed, is precisely the electrical power delivered plus the losses, which is the energy accounting of every generator ever built.

There are two ways to write the same physics, and both are useful. The flux-linkage form above suits a coil in a changing field. The motional form, e equals B times l times v, gives the voltage induced in a conductor of length l metres moving at velocity v metres per second at right angles to a magnetic flux density B in teslas. A conductor 0.3 m long sweeping through a 0.8 T field at 40 m/s develops 0.3 × 0.8 × 40, that is 9.6 volts. Since real machines have hundreds of such conductors in series in each winding, useful voltages are reached easily. Three quantities therefore set the output of any generator: how strong the magnetic field is, how much conductor is exposed to it, and how fast the two move relative to one another. Every design decision in the rest of the machine is ultimately about maximising one of those three, or about coping with the heat, stress and losses that maximising them creates. Practical flux densities are limited to roughly 1.5 to 2.0 T by the saturation of iron, which is why generators cannot simply be made stronger by winding on more field current indefinitely.

sections.heading: From a Spinning Loop to a Machine: Slip Rings and Commutators
sections.body:
The textbook starting point is a single rectangular loop of wire rotating in a uniform magnetic field between two poles. As it turns, the flux through it varies as the cosine of the angle, so by Faraday's law the induced voltage varies as the sine. At the instant the loop lies in the plane of the field, the conductors cut flux at maximum rate and the voltage peaks; a quarter turn later the loop is perpendicular to the field, the conductors move parallel to the flux lines, and the voltage is zero. One revolution produces one complete sine wave. The output is inherently alternating, which is a consequence of geometry rather than a design choice. Getting direct current out of a rotating machine requires extra apparatus; getting alternating current out is what happens naturally.

Two mechanisms exist to get the power off a rotating member. Slip rings are continuous conducting rings on the shaft, one per winding end, with stationary carbon brushes riding on them. Each ring stays permanently connected to the same end of the winding, so whatever waveform exists in the winding appears unchanged at the brushes; slip rings pass alternating current out as alternating current. A commutator is different. It is a cylinder split into insulated copper segments, arranged so that as the loop passes through the position where its voltage reverses, the brushes simultaneously swap which segment they contact. The reversal in the winding and the reversal of the connection cancel, and the external circuit sees a voltage of constant polarity. The commutator is a mechanical rectifier, and it was the only rectifier available before the 1900s.

Both approaches have consequences that shape real machines. A single-loop output is a poor sine wave with a commutator, being a series of humps rather than a smooth level, so practical DC machines use many loops spread around the armature feeding many commutator segments, which reduces the ripple to a few per cent. More significantly, brushes and commutators wear, spark, generate carbon dust and radio interference, limit the safe peripheral speed of the rotor, and require regular maintenance. This is the central reason that modern alternators invert the arrangement: instead of rotating the power-producing winding and taking heavy current off through sliding contacts, they rotate the magnetic field and leave the power winding stationary in the stator. The field circuit carries only a small fraction of the machine's power, perhaps one to three per cent, so if any sliding contact is needed at all it is small, and the full output current is taken from fixed terminals with no moving joint. That single inversion is what allowed alternators to be built at hundreds of megawatts and tens of kilovolts.

sections.heading: Inside the Machine: Stator, Rotor, Air Gap and Iron
sections.body:
Cut open any rotating electrical machine and the same parts appear. The stator is the stationary outer assembly: a cylindrical stack of steel laminations with slots cut in its inner face, carrying the windings, held in a frame that also provides the bearing housings and cooling paths. The rotor is the rotating inner member on the shaft, again usually laminated steel, carrying either a field winding or permanent magnets. Between them is the air gap, typically 0.5 to 3 mm in small machines and up to 20 to 30 mm in a large turbine generator. The air gap is the single most influential dimension in the design: magnetic reluctance is concentrated there, so halving it roughly halves the field current needed for the same flux, but too small a gap risks the rotor rubbing the stator under thermal expansion, shaft deflection or bearing wear.

The iron is laminated for a specific reason. A solid steel core sitting in a changing magnetic field has voltages induced in the iron itself, driving eddy currents that circulate and dissipate power as heat. Slicing the core into thin sheets, typically 0.35 to 0.65 mm thick, each coated with an insulating varnish or oxide, breaks up the paths those currents could take. Eddy loss falls roughly with the square of the lamination thickness, so this is extremely effective. The steel itself is a silicon-alloyed electrical steel, with silicon at around 2 to 3.5 per cent raising the resistivity and reducing loss further, at the cost of making the sheet brittle. The second iron loss is hysteresis, the energy consumed each cycle in reversing the magnetic domains, which is proportional to frequency and to the area of the material's B-H loop. Together, eddy and hysteresis losses are called core loss or iron loss, and they are present whenever the machine is energised, whether or not it is delivering any output.

The windings are copper conductors laid in the slots, insulated from the iron and from each other. In a modern alternator the stator carries three separate windings physically spaced 120 degrees apart around the bore, which is what produces three-phase output. Insulation is classified by the temperature it will tolerate: Class B to 130 °C, Class F to 155 °C and Class H to 180 °C are the common grades, and the rating plate normally quotes both the insulation class and the permitted temperature rise, often Class H insulation operated to Class F rise as a deliberate margin. The rule of thumb, derived from the Arrhenius relation, is that insulation life roughly halves for every 8 to 10 °C of sustained overtemperature, which is why cooling and load management matter far more to a generator's lifespan than anything else the owner controls. The number of magnetic poles is the other defining parameter: a two-pole rotor has one north and one south, a four-pole has two of each, and the pole count together with shaft speed fixes the output frequency.

sections.heading: The Synchronous Alternator: Rotating Field, Three Phases, Fixed Frequency
sections.body:
The synchronous alternator is the machine that generates nearly all grid electricity, and its defining arrangement is the rotating field. A direct current is fed into a winding on the rotor, making it an electromagnet with a fixed number of north and south poles. The prime mover spins that magnet, and the sweeping field induces alternating voltages in the three stator windings. Because the windings are spaced 120 degrees apart around the bore, their voltages peak one third of a cycle apart, producing a balanced three-phase supply. Three-phase is used because it delivers constant total instantaneous power rather than the pulsating power of a single phase, needs less conductor material for the same power, and produces a rotating field in any motor connected to it, which is why three-phase motors self-start.

The word synchronous means the rotor speed and the electrical frequency are rigidly locked. The relationship is f equals P times N divided by 120, where f is frequency in hertz, P is the number of poles and N is shaft speed in revolutions per minute. A two-pole machine must turn at 3,000 rpm for 50 Hz or 3,600 rpm for 60 Hz; a four-pole machine at 1,500 or 1,800 rpm respectively. This is why standby gensets in Europe run at 1,500 rpm and in North America at 1,800 rpm, and why large steam turbine generators are two-pole machines whose rotors turn at 3,000 rpm with a surface speed at the rotor body of well over 500 km/h, a mechanical design problem in itself. Slow prime movers force the opposite choice: a hydro generator turning at 100 rpm needs 60 poles for 50 Hz, which is why hydro alternators are large-diameter, short-axial machines with a ring of salient poles bolted to a spider.

That geometry difference has a name. Cylindrical-rotor or non-salient machines have the field winding buried in slots in a smooth forged rotor, and are used for two- and four-pole high-speed turbo-generators where protruding poles would be destroyed by windage and centrifugal stress. Salient-pole machines have distinct poles projecting from the hub, are cheaper and simpler, and are used for everything slower: hydro sets, engine-driven gensets and most alternators below a few megawatts. Salient poles make the machine magnetically unequal along and between the poles, which is described by two different reactances, direct-axis and quadrature-axis, and gives such machines a small reluctance torque even with no field current. Almost all synchronous machines also carry a damper or amortisseur winding, a set of copper or brass bars shorted at the ends and buried in the pole faces. It does nothing in steady operation but opposes any momentary difference between rotor speed and field speed, damping the shaft oscillations, called hunting, that would otherwise follow every load change.

sections.heading: Excitation: Where the Rotor's Magnetism Comes From
sections.body:
A synchronous alternator needs direct current in its rotor winding to create the magnetic field, and how that current gets onto a spinning shaft is one of the defining engineering problems of the machine. It is not a trivial amount of power: excitation typically consumes half a per cent to three per cent of machine rating, so a 1,000 kW generator may need 10 to 30 kW of field power, at perhaps 60 to 250 volts DC. Crucially, the field current also controls the output voltage, because output is proportional to flux. Vary the field and you vary the terminal voltage, which is the mechanism by which every alternator regulates itself.

The oldest arrangement is brushed excitation: two slip rings on the shaft, carbon brushes riding on them, and a controlled DC supply. It is simple and the field is directly accessible for testing, but the brushes wear, produce dust that can track across insulation, spark in flammable atmospheres and need periodic inspection. The dominant modern arrangement is brushless excitation, and it is worth understanding because it looks paradoxical. A small auxiliary alternator, the exciter, is built on the same shaft but inside out: its field winding is stationary and its armature rotates. The exciter's three-phase output therefore appears on the rotating member already, where a set of rotating diodes bolted to the shaft rectifies it to DC and feeds the main field directly. No sliding contact exists anywhere in the power path. Control is exercised on the exciter's stationary field winding, which needs only tens of watts.

Two refinements complete the picture. The permanent magnet pilot exciter, or PMG, is a third small machine with permanent magnets on the shaft, providing a supply for the control electronics that is completely independent of the main output. This matters enormously under fault conditions: a machine with only self-excitation loses its control power when its terminals are short-circuited and cannot then deliver the sustained fault current needed to blow the fuse or trip the breaker that would clear the fault. A PMG-equipped set typically sustains around three times rated current for ten seconds, which is a specification worth checking on any installation with selective protection. The second refinement is the automatic voltage regulator, or AVR, an electronic controller that measures output voltage, compares it with a setpoint and adjusts exciter field current to correct the error, typically holding the output within plus or minus 0.5 to 1 per cent from no load to full load. Machines without a PMG rely on residual magnetism in the rotor iron to start the build-up process, which is why a machine that has stood idle for years, been struck by lightning or been connected in reverse polarity may fail to produce any output at all and require flashing of the field, a brief application of a battery to re-establish that residual magnetism.

sections.heading: The Automotive Alternator: Claw Poles, Diodes and a Regulator
sections.body:
The alternator under a car bonnet is the most numerous synchronous machine on earth, produced in hundreds of millions per year, and it is a beautiful piece of cost engineering. Its job is to supply the vehicle's electrical load and recharge the battery across a speed range of perhaps 1,800 to 18,000 alternator rpm, a ten-to-one range, while producing an output steady enough for electronics. Typical output is 70 to 180 amperes at around 14 volts in a passenger car, so 1 to 2.5 kW, with 24-volt systems in trucks and outputs to 250 A or more in vehicles with heavy accessory loads. Before the mid-1960s cars used DC dynamos; alternators displaced them almost entirely once silicon rectifier diodes became cheap, because they produce useful output at idle, need no commutator, and are lighter for the same power.

The rotor is the distinctive part: a Lundell or claw-pole design, in which a single simple cylindrical field coil is sandwiched between two steel end-pieces whose interleaved fingers form alternating north and south poles, usually six pairs, that is twelve poles. One cheap winding thus produces a multi-pole field that would otherwise need twelve separate coils. Field current, typically 3 to 5 A, reaches it through two small slip rings and brushes, which carry only that small current and last for perhaps 150,000 to 250,000 km. The stator is a conventional three-phase winding, usually in a delta or wye connection, and the three-phase output goes to a six-diode bridge rectifier bolted to a finned heat sink. Six-diode full-wave three-phase rectification gives a DC output whose ripple is only about 4 per cent of the mean, which the battery smooths almost completely. Many designs add a second pair of diodes on a neutral tap to recover a little extra output.

Voltage regulation is done not by controlling the output but by controlling the field. The regulator, a small solid-state module usually integral with the brush holder, switches field current on and off at a few hundred hertz, varying the duty cycle to hold system voltage at a setpoint. That setpoint is not a constant: it is temperature-compensated, typically around 14.4 to 14.7 V when cold and falling to about 13.8 V when hot, because lead-acid batteries need a higher charge voltage at low temperature and will gas and lose water if overcharged when warm. Modern vehicles go further, with the engine control unit commanding the alternator over a LIN bus to raise output during braking and reduce it during acceleration, a mild form of energy recovery. Two practical facts follow from all this. First, an alternator will not build up output if the field circuit is open, which is why the charge warning lamp is wired in series with the field on many designs and a blown bulb can stop charging entirely. Second, disconnecting the battery while the engine runs is a bad test: the battery is the load that damps the system, and removing it can cause a load-dump voltage transient of 60 to 120 V that destroys electronics.

sections.heading: DC Generators and Dynamos: Commutation and Its Limits
sections.body:
Before the alternator won, the DC generator or dynamo was the standard machine, and it is worth understanding both historically and because DC machines remain in service in traction, some marine systems and legacy installations. In a DC generator the arrangement is the opposite of an alternator: the field is stationary, produced by poles bolted to the inside of the yoke, and the armature carrying the generated power rotates, with its many coils connected to a commutator. The commutator segments, made of hard-drawn copper separated by mica, mechanically reverse the connection at the right instant to produce unidirectional output. Because the full output current passes through the brush-to-commutator interface, a large DC machine carries a substantial and continually wearing sliding contact, and that is the fundamental limitation.

DC generators are classified by how the field is supplied. A separately excited machine takes field current from an outside source, giving the most flexible control. A shunt generator connects the field across its own armature, so it self-excites: residual magnetism in the poles produces a small voltage, which drives a small field current, which increases the flux, and the process bootstraps until the field resistance line intersects the machine's magnetisation curve. This self-excitation only works if the shunt field is connected with the right polarity, if the field resistance is below a critical value and if the machine turns the right way, which is why a reconnected or reversed dynamo often refuses to build up. A series generator carries the load current through a few heavy field turns, so its voltage rises with load, useful only in specialised applications such as the old constant-current street-lighting circuits. Compound generators combine both windings; a cumulatively compounded machine can be made to hold nearly constant terminal voltage from no load to full load, which was the classic solution before electronic regulators existed.

The reason DC generators disappeared is commutation. As current is transferred from segment to segment, the coil being switched has its current reversed in a fraction of a millisecond, and the inductance of that coil opposes the change, producing an arc at the trailing brush edge. Uncorrected, this burns the commutator and limits the machine severely. The fixes are interpoles, small auxiliary poles between the main ones carrying load current and generating exactly the voltage needed to drive the reversal, and on large machines compensating windings buried in the pole faces to cancel armature reaction. All of this is expensive, and none of it removes the wear, the carbon dust, the fire risk in dusty or flammable atmospheres, the radio interference or the speed limit imposed by the commutator's mechanical strength. Once semiconductor rectifiers made it trivial to convert AC to DC electronically, there was no remaining reason to do it mechanically, and DC generation was abandoned for new designs by the 1970s.

sections.heading: Induction and Doubly-Fed Generators: Machines Without a DC Field
sections.body:
A third family exists that has no DC field circuit at all. An induction machine, also called asynchronous, has a stator winding like any other and a rotor that is usually a squirrel cage, a set of solid aluminium or copper bars shorted by end rings. There is no electrical connection to the rotor whatsoever. When such a machine is connected to a live three-phase supply and driven above the synchronous speed set by the supply frequency, it delivers real power to the supply and acts as a generator. The difference between actual rotor speed and synchronous speed, expressed as a fraction, is called slip, and it is negative in generating mode, typically between minus 1 and minus 5 per cent. A 1,500 rpm nominal machine generating at rated output might turn at 1,545 rpm.

The attractions are cost and robustness. An induction generator is simply a standard induction motor, made by the million, with no brushes, no slip rings, no exciter, no AVR and no synchronising equipment: connect it and drive it above synchronous speed and it generates, and it cannot fall out of step because it was never in step. The corresponding drawback is that it produces no magnetising current of its own and must draw reactive power, typically 30 to 50 per cent of its rating in kVAr, from somewhere else. Connected to a strong grid, that is free. Standing alone, it needs a capacitor bank across the terminals to supply the reactive current, which is the self-excited induction generator or SEIG used in small stand-alone hydro and wind schemes. Self-excitation is finicky: the capacitance must exceed a critical value that depends on speed and load, the machine relies on residual rotor magnetism to start, and both voltage and frequency wander with load and speed unless a separate controller manages them, so the SEIG is best suited to loads that tolerate variation, such as heating.

Wind power gave induction generators their most sophisticated form. In a doubly-fed induction generator, or DFIG, the rotor is wound rather than a cage and its terminals are brought out through slip rings to a bidirectional power converter. Because the converter only has to handle the slip power, roughly 25 to 30 per cent of machine rating for a plus or minus 30 per cent speed range, it is far cheaper than a converter carrying the full output. Controlling the magnitude, frequency and phase of the rotor injection lets the machine run at variable speed while delivering fixed-frequency power at controllable power factor, which is exactly what a turbine tracking the wind needs. DFIGs dominated wind turbines from the late 1990s through roughly the 2010s. They are now being displaced in new designs by direct-drive or medium-speed permanent magnet synchronous generators feeding a full-rating converter, which eliminate the slip rings and gearbox and cope better with grid faults, at the price of a larger converter and of relying on rare-earth magnet material.

sections.heading: Armature Reaction, Synchronous Reactance and Voltage Regulation
sections.body:
An unloaded alternator produces a voltage set purely by field current and speed. The moment current flows in the stator, that current creates its own magnetic field, which adds vectorially to the field from the rotor. This effect is called armature reaction, and it is the reason terminal voltage sags under load. Its character depends on the phase of the current. With a purely resistive load the stator field is mostly cross-magnetising, distorting the flux distribution sideways with modest effect on its magnitude. With a lagging, that is inductive, load the stator field opposes the rotor field directly and is strongly demagnetising, so terminal voltage falls markedly. With a leading, that is capacitive, load the effect reverses and is magnetising, and terminal voltage can actually rise above its no-load value, which is a real hazard on long lightly loaded cables.

Engineers fold armature reaction together with the winding's own leakage inductance into a single equivalent quantity called synchronous reactance, symbol Xs, and model the machine as an ideal internal voltage E behind that reactance in series with the winding resistance R. The terminal voltage is then V equals E minus the current times the complex impedance R plus jXs. Synchronous reactance is large by the standards of most circuits, commonly 1.0 to 2.0 per unit, meaning that rated current through it would drop a voltage equal to or greater than rated voltage. This has a useful consequence: the sustained short-circuit current of a synchronous machine is only about 1 divided by Xs in per unit, that is roughly 0.5 to 1 times rated current, far less than a transformer of similar rating would deliver. The initial current is much higher, governed by the subtransient reactance Xd double-prime of typically 0.12 to 0.20 per unit, decaying over a few cycles to the transient value Xd prime and over a second or two to the synchronous value.

Voltage regulation as a specification means the percentage rise in terminal voltage when full load is thrown off, calculated as no-load voltage minus full-load voltage, divided by full-load voltage, times a hundred. For an unregulated machine at a lagging power factor of 0.8 this can easily be 20 to 40 per cent, which is unusable, and it is precisely why every practical alternator has an automatic voltage regulator continuously trimming field current to hold the terminals steady, typically within plus or minus 0.5 per cent in steady state. Two dynamic figures matter more than the steady-state one when specifying a set. Transient voltage dip is how far the voltage falls at the instant a large load is applied, commonly 15 to 25 per cent for a step load, and recovery time is how long the AVR takes to restore it, typically one to three seconds. Motor starting is the usual test case, since a direct-on-line induction motor draws six to eight times its running current for several seconds at a very poor power factor, which is close to the worst thing you can do to a generator's voltage.

sections.heading: Real Power, Reactive Power and the Load Angle
sections.body:
Operating a generator requires distinguishing two things that both look like output. Real power, measured in watts or kilowatts, is the rate of actual energy delivery, and it must be supplied mechanically by the prime mover: every kilowatt out of the terminals is a kilowatt plus losses that the engine or turbine must produce. Reactive power, measured in volt-amperes reactive or kVAr, is energy that sloshes back and forth between the generator and inductive or capacitive elements of the load without net transfer, and it is supplied not by the prime mover but by the excitation system. Apparent power, in volt-amperes or kVA, is the vector sum, and it is what actually heats the windings, which is why alternators are rated in kVA rather than kW. Power factor is the ratio of real to apparent power, the cosine of the angle between voltage and current, and generator sets are conventionally rated at 0.8 lagging: a 100 kVA set is a 80 kW set.

The mechanism controlling real power in a machine connected to a grid is the load angle, usually written as delta, the angular difference between the rotor's magnetic axis and the rotating field of the system. Push harder on the shaft and the rotor advances a few electrical degrees ahead of the system field; the machine then delivers power according to P equals E times V divided by Xs, all multiplied by the sine of delta. This sine relationship is the most consequential equation in power system stability. Power rises with load angle up to delta equals 90 degrees, where it reaches the steady-state stability limit, and beyond that point further advance produces less power, not more, so the rotor accelerates away, loses synchronism and the machine pole-slips, an event violent enough to damage shafts and requiring immediate disconnection. Machines are normally operated at load angles well under 30 degrees to leave margin for disturbances.

Reactive power is controlled independently, by field current. On an isolated machine, raising the field raises the voltage. On a machine locked to a large grid the voltage is fixed by the grid, so raising the field cannot change it and instead pushes reactive power out: the machine becomes overexcited and supplies kVAr, helping hold up system voltage. Reduce the field and it becomes underexcited and absorbs kVAr. Plotting the safe combinations of real and reactive power gives the capability curve printed in every machine manual, bounded on three sides by different limits: the field winding's thermal limit at high excitation, the stator winding's thermal limit at high apparent power, and at low excitation both the stability limit and, in large turbo-generators, heating of the stator end iron by leakage flux. Operating outside that curve overheats something that is difficult and expensive to repair, which is why the two control loops on a generator control panel, governor for kilowatts and AVR for volts and kVAr, are the two independent handles the operator actually has.

sections.heading: Synchronising and Running Machines in Parallel
sections.body:
Connecting an alternator to a live system, or connecting two alternators together, cannot be done by simply closing a switch. A mismatch dumps enormous current through both machines and applies a torque impulse to both shafts and couplings that can shear keys, crack crankshafts and destroy windings. Four conditions must be satisfied simultaneously before the breaker closes. The voltages must be equal, in practice within about 0.5 to 5 per cent. The frequencies must be equal, in practice with the incoming machine running very slightly fast, by 0.1 to 0.2 Hz, so that on closing it immediately picks up a little load rather than being motored. The phase angle must match, ideally within 5 to 10 electrical degrees. And the phase sequence, the order in which the three phases reach their peaks, must be identical, which is checked once at installation and never changes unless someone reconnects the cables.

The traditional instruments are three lamps connected across the open breaker poles, which go dark together at the moment of coincidence in the dark-lamp method, and the synchroscope, a rotating pointer whose speed shows the frequency difference and whose position shows the phase angle. A pointer creeping slowly clockwise means the incoming machine is slightly fast, which is what you want; the breaker is closed a moment before the pointer reaches the twelve o'clock position, to allow for breaker closing time of typically 50 to 150 milliseconds. Modern installations use an automatic synchroniser that adjusts the incoming set's governor and AVR and issues the close command itself, and a check-synchronising relay that independently blocks the breaker unless the conditions are genuinely met. That second, independent device exists because out-of-phase closure is one of the most destructive single errors possible in a power plant.

Once paralleled, the question becomes how machines share load, and here a subtlety catches people out. Opening the throttle on one machine in a parallel group does not make it run faster, because the system holds its speed; it makes it take more of the real load. Similarly, raising its excitation does not raise system voltage; it makes that machine take more of the reactive load. Stable sharing is achieved with droop, a deliberate slope in the control characteristics. Speed droop of typically 3 to 5 per cent means the governor targets a speed that falls linearly with load, so if one machine takes more load it slows slightly and naturally sheds some back to the others; reactive droop, sometimes called a quadrature droop or cross-current compensation, does the equivalent for kVAr and prevents the machines from fighting each other with circulating reactive current. A single machine running alone is instead run isochronous, holding exactly constant speed at all loads. Many modern controllers do both, switching from isochronous to droop automatically when a second machine comes on line.

sections.heading: Prime Movers, Governors and What Sets the Frequency
sections.body:
The generator sets the voltage; the prime mover sets the frequency, because frequency is rigidly tied to shaft speed. Whatever turns the shaft therefore needs a speed control system, and that system's quality determines the electrical quality of the supply. Diesel engines dominate standby and prime power up to a few megawatts, being cheap per kilowatt, tolerant of load steps and quick to start, with a typical set reaching full load within 10 seconds of a start command, which is why they back up hospitals and data centres. Gas engines and gas turbines serve continuous generation and combined heat and power; a gas turbine has poor part-load efficiency but excellent power density. Steam turbines dominate large thermal and nuclear stations. Hydro turbines, whether Pelton, Francis or Kaplan, offer the fastest and most controllable response of all. Wind turbines are the awkward case, since their input is uncontrollable, which is why they need either variable-speed electronics or blade pitch control, and usually both.

The governor is the speed controller. Mechanical governors, descended from James Watt's centrifugal flyball design of 1788, used spinning weights whose outward movement closed the throttle, and gave droop characteristics of a few per cent with sluggish response. Modern electronic governors read a magnetic pickup counting flywheel teeth, compute an error against setpoint and drive an actuator or, on common-rail engines, command fuel quantity directly, typically holding steady-state speed within plus or minus 0.25 per cent. Standards classify this: ISO 8528 defines governing classes G1 to G4, where G1 suits simple loads such as lighting and heating, G2 covers general commercial use, G3 is required for sensitive electronic equipment and G4 is a specified special case. Buying a set rated for the wrong class is a common and expensive procurement mistake.

The hardest specification to meet is block load acceptance, and it is where engine and alternator interact. When a large load is applied instantaneously, the alternator demands the torque immediately but the engine cannot respond immediately, particularly a turbocharged diesel, because the turbocharger must spool up before enough air is available to burn the extra fuel, a lag of one to several seconds known as turbo lag. Speed therefore dips, and with it frequency, before the governor recovers. Typical figures are a transient frequency dip of 5 to 10 per cent recovering within 3 to 5 seconds, and a well-specified set will state the maximum step load it will accept in one go, often around 50 to 70 per cent of rating for a modern turbocharged unit. Two consequences follow for real installations. Large motor loads should be started in sequence, or through soft starters or variable-speed drives, rather than all at once. And running a diesel set at very light load for long periods, below roughly 30 per cent of rating, causes incomplete combustion, unburnt fuel and oil glazing the cylinder bores, a condition called wet stacking that ruins engines and is avoided by load banking the set periodically to at least 50 to 75 per cent for an hour or two.

sections.heading: Ratings, Losses, Cooling and Efficiency
sections.body:
A generator's rating plate is a contract, and reading it correctly avoids most of the mistakes made in specifying and operating one. The apparent power rating in kVA is the primary number, because heating depends on current regardless of phase angle. The kW figure alongside it assumes the stated power factor, conventionally 0.8 lagging, so a 500 kVA set is a 400 kW set and delivering 500 kW from it is not possible even if the engine could manage it. Duty ratings matter as much: standby power is a rating for emergency use at varying load for a limited number of hours per year, typically under 200, with no overload capability; prime power permits unlimited hours at varying load with a defined average, commonly 70 per cent of rating, and usually a 10 per cent overload for one hour in twelve; continuous power permits unlimited hours at constant full load and is the most conservative and expensive rating for the same hardware.

Losses divide into five categories, and knowing them tells you where the heat is. Copper or I-squared-R losses occur in the stator and field windings and rise with the square of current, so they dominate at full load. Core losses, comprising hysteresis and eddy currents in the iron, are roughly constant once the machine is excited. Stray load losses arise from leakage flux causing eddy currents in structural steel and are hard to calculate, usually taken as around 0.5 to 1 per cent. Windage and friction come from the cooling fan, bearings and air drag on the rotor, and are significant in high-speed machines. Excitation losses account for the field power itself. Efficiency for the alternator alone is high, commonly 90 to 95 per cent for small machines and 97 to over 99 per cent for very large turbo-generators. The overall efficiency of a genset is quite another matter, because it is dominated by the engine: a good diesel set converts 35 to 42 per cent of fuel energy into electricity, and the rest leaves as exhaust and coolant heat, which combined heat and power schemes exist to recover.

Cooling is the practical constraint on how much power a given frame will deliver. Small and medium machines use open ventilated or drip-proof enclosures with a shaft-mounted fan pulling ambient air through the windings, and their ratings assume a stated ambient, usually 40 °C, and altitude, usually up to 1,000 m. Derating is required beyond these: roughly 3 per cent of output per 500 m of additional altitude because thinner air cools less well, and around 2 to 3 per cent per 5 °C above the reference ambient. Larger machines use closed-circuit air-to-air or air-to-water heat exchangers, designated by IC codes, and the largest turbo-generators use hydrogen at 3 to 5 bar, chosen because it has about fourteen times the thermal conductivity of air and roughly one fourteenth the density, so it cools better and causes far less windage loss, at the price of a hydrogen seal-oil system and a serious explosion risk requiring purge procedures. The very largest have water circulating directly through hollow stator conductors.

sections.heading: Installing and Commissioning a Set: A Working Procedure
sections.body: Most generator failures in service trace back to installation and commissioning rather than to the machine itself. The list below is the sequence a competent commissioning engineer follows for an engine-driven standby set, and the same logic scales to larger machines. Where local electrical regulations apply, they override anything here, and connection to premises wiring or to a utility supply is work that in most jurisdictions must be done by a licensed person.
ingredients: The machine's own documentation: rating plate data, wiring diagram, AVR manual and the manufacturer's commissioning checklist, which will list torque figures and setpoints specific to that model.
An insulation resistance tester (megger) rated at 500 V for machines up to 600 V, plus a low-resistance ohmmeter for winding and earth-bond checks.
A true-RMS multimeter, a clamp meter covering the full expected current, and a phase-rotation tester.
A resistive load bank sized to at least 75 per cent of set rating, hired if necessary; commissioning without one proves almost nothing about behaviour under real load.
Anti-vibration mounts, flexible exhaust bellows and flexible fuel lines, since rigid connections transmit vibration and crack.
Earthing conductors and electrode, plus the correct transfer switch or mechanical interlock if the set will supply an installation that also has a utility supply.
steps: Confirm the site: firm level foundation carrying the wet weight, at least 1 m clearance for airflow and service access, and an exhaust discharging clear of every window, door and air intake.
Measure insulation resistance winding to earth with a 500 V megger; below about 1 megohm on a low-voltage machine means it is damp and must be dried before energising, not tested harder.
Verify the mechanical build: coupling alignment within tolerance, guards fitted, mounts secure and all fixings torqued to specification.
Complete the fluids: correct engine oil, coolant at the right antifreeze concentration, clean fuel, and bleed the fuel system fully to remove air.
Decide deliberately whether the alternator star point is earthed at the set or elsewhere, since two bonds create circulating currents and none leaves the installation unprotected.
Prove the phase rotation and the polarity of every current transformer before energising any protection or attempting to parallel anything.
Start the set off load and let it stabilise. Check voltage on all phases and between phases, frequency, oil pressure, coolant temperature, and listen for anything unusual before proceeding.
Apply load in steps with the load bank at 25, 50, 75 and 100 per cent, holding each until temperatures stabilise, and record voltage, current per phase, frequency, power factor and temperatures.
Test the transient response by applying and removing the largest realistic step load, recording voltage dip, frequency dip and both recovery times against the specification.
Prove every protection individually: overspeed, low oil pressure, high coolant temperature, overcurrent, reverse power where fitted, and the emergency stop.
Test the automatic start and transfer sequence end to end by removing the utility supply, and confirm no load is ever connected to two sources at once.
Record everything in a commissioning report and leave the machine on a documented routine of monthly off-load runs and periodic on-load exercise.

sections.heading: Faults, Diagnosis and What Goes Wrong
sections.body:
Generator faults fall into recognisable families. No output at all on a machine that turns normally is usually an excitation problem. On a self-excited set the commonest cause is loss of residual magnetism after long storage, reverse rotation or a lightning event; the remedy is flashing the field, briefly applying a 12 V battery through a resistor to the field with correct polarity while the set runs. Other causes are a failed AVR, an open field circuit, worn brushes on a brushed machine, or a failed rotating diode. Diode failure on a brushless machine has two distinct signatures worth knowing: an open-circuit diode gives reduced and unstable output, while a short-circuited one usually gives very low output and heavy heating, and both can be found by measuring exciter field current, which will be abnormally high with a shorted diode.

Voltage that is present but wrong divides by symptom. Voltage low across all phases but stable suggests the AVR setpoint, an underspeed condition, or overload; check frequency first, because low frequency almost always means an engine problem masquerading as an electrical one, and note that most AVRs deliberately reduce voltage in proportion to frequency below a knee point, the volts-per-hertz function, to protect against saturation. Voltage unstable or hunting suggests AVR gain set too high, a poor speed signal, or a governor fighting the AVR. Voltage unbalanced between phases points at unbalanced single-phase loading, a winding fault, or a loose connection; unbalance above about 2 per cent causes negative-sequence current that induces double-frequency currents in the rotor and heats it rapidly, which is why large machines carry dedicated negative-sequence protection. Overvoltage, which is more destructive than undervoltage, points at AVR failure or loss of sensing, and should trip the set.

The failure modes that destroy machines are worth naming explicitly. Winding insulation failure is the commonest end of life, driven by sustained overtemperature, moisture ingress in machines that stand unheated, contamination by oil and conductive dust, and mechanical abrasion from vibration or loose slot wedges; anti-condensation heaters and regular insulation testing address most of it. Bearing failure follows from misalignment, wrong grease or, in machines fed from or near power electronics, shaft currents that pit the races, addressed with an insulated bearing at the non-drive end or a shaft grounding brush. Loss of excitation causes a synchronous machine on a grid to run as an induction generator, drawing heavy reactive current and overheating the rotor within seconds to minutes, which is why loss-of-field protection exists. Motoring, where the prime mover fails and the machine draws power from the system, is harmless to the alternator but can wreck a steam turbine by overheating its blades in seconds, hence reverse-power protection. And out-of-phase paralleling remains the single most violent electrical mistake available, which is why the interlocks that prevent it should never be defeated to save time.

guides.title: Transformers
guides.summary: The electromagnetic transformer from first principles to practice: induction physics, the ideal and real transformer, core materials and losses, construction, grid-scale and electronic applications, high-frequency designs, ratings, testing, and how transformers fail.
guides.safetyNote: Transformers connect to lethal voltages. Mains and grid-side windings can kill on contact, capacitors and long cable runs can hold charge after disconnection, and a current transformer with its secondary open-circuited while the primary is energized can develop thousands of volts. Never work on an energized transformer, always verify isolation with a meter you have tested on a known live source, and never open-circuit an energized current transformer secondary.

sections.heading: What a Transformer Is and Why It Matters
sections.body: A transformer is a machine with no moving parts that transfers electrical power from one circuit to another through a shared magnetic field, changing the voltage and current along the way while leaving the power, minus small losses, unchanged. It is arguably the device that made the modern electrical world possible. The reason is a stubborn piece of physics: when current flows through a wire, power is lost as heat in proportion to the square of the current times the resistance of the wire. Double the current and you quadruple the loss. To move large amounts of power over long distances economically, you must therefore move it at low current, which for a given power means high voltage; but high voltage is lethal and useless at the point of consumption, where lamps, motors, and electronics need tens or hundreds of volts, not hundreds of thousands. The transformer resolves the contradiction: it steps voltage up for transmission and back down for use, cheaply, silently, and with efficiencies that in large units exceed ninety-nine percent, among the highest of any machine humans build. This capability decided the outcome of the so-called war of the currents in the 1880s. Thomas Edison's direct-current system could not change voltage easily and so could serve customers only within a mile or two of each power station. The alternating-current system championed by George Westinghouse and Nikola Tesla, built on transformer designs by Lucien Gaulard and John Gibbs and perfected in 1885 by the Hungarian engineers Karoly Zipernowsky, Otto Blathy, and Miksa Deri, and independently by William Stanley in Massachusetts, could generate at a convenient voltage, transmit at a high one, and deliver at a safe one. Alternating current won, and the closed-core transformer of 1885 is recognizably the same device that hums in substations today. The scale of its deployment is hard to overstate: a typical unit of electrical energy is transformed five or more times between generator and wall socket, through a step-up transformer at the power plant raising perhaps twenty thousand volts to four hundred thousand, several substation transformers stepping down in stages, and finally a distribution transformer on a pole or pad delivering the local mains voltage of one hundred twenty or two hundred thirty volts. Beyond the grid, transformers isolate patients from mains in medical equipment, match microphones to amplifiers, weld steel, ignite gas furnaces, and, in miniaturized high-frequency form, sit inside every phone charger made. The same physics scales from units the size of a fingernail handling a fraction of a watt to single machines the size of a house rated over a thousand megavolt-amperes and weighing four hundred tonnes. Understanding transformers means understanding one elegant idea, electromagnetic induction between coupled coils, and then the long series of practical consequences, imperfections, and engineering compromises that follow from embodying that idea in copper, iron, insulation, and oil.

sections.heading: The Physics: Induction, Faraday's Law, and Lenz's Law
sections.body: Everything a transformer does follows from two discoveries of the early nineteenth century. In 1820 Hans Christian Orsted found that an electric current creates a magnetic field around its conductor, and in 1831 Michael Faraday found the converse: a changing magnetic field passing through a loop of wire drives a voltage in that loop. Faraday's law states the relationship precisely: the voltage induced in a coil equals the number of turns in the coil multiplied by the rate of change of the magnetic flux threading it. Flux, measured in webers, is the amount of magnetic field passing through the loop's area; one weber changing in one second induces one volt per turn. The crucial word is changing. A steady field induces nothing, which is why transformers work only on alternating or otherwise varying current and why a transformer connected to direct current does nothing useful except overheat. Lenz's law, formulated by Heinrich Lenz in 1834, supplies the direction: the induced voltage always drives current in whatever direction opposes the change in flux that created it. This is not a bookkeeping convention but energy conservation in disguise, and it is what makes a transformer self-regulating, as becomes clear when a load is connected. Now assemble the device. Wind two electrically separate coils, called the primary and the secondary, around a common core of magnetic material. Apply an alternating voltage to the primary. A small current, called the magnetizing current, flows and establishes an alternating flux in the core. Because the core guides essentially all of this flux through both coils, the same flux change threads every turn of both windings, inducing the same voltage per turn everywhere. A coil with more turns therefore shows a proportionally higher total voltage, and one with fewer turns a lower one; this is the entire secret of voltage transformation. In the primary, the induced voltage, often called the back electromotive force, almost exactly cancels the applied voltage, which is why the unloaded magnetizing current stays small, typically a few percent of rated current. When a load is connected to the secondary, secondary current flows, and by Lenz's law that current creates magnetomotive force opposing the core flux. The slight resulting dip in back EMF lets the primary draw more current from the supply, restoring the flux and delivering the power. Primary current thus rises automatically and exactly in step with secondary demand, with no controller of any kind: the magnetic field itself is the messenger. One more consequence of Faraday's law shapes all transformer design. For a sinusoidal supply, the required flux is inversely proportional to frequency, captured in the transformer EMF equation: RMS voltage equals 4.44 times frequency times turns times peak flux. Halve the frequency and the core needs twice the flux, which is why a sixty-hertz transformer may saturate on a fifty-hertz supply, and why raising frequency into the kilohertz range, as switch-mode power supplies do, shrinks transformers dramatically.

sections.heading: The Ideal Transformer: Turns Ratio, Current, and Impedance
sections.body: Engineers begin analysis with the ideal transformer, an abstraction that captures the essential behavior before imperfections are added back. An ideal transformer has windings with zero resistance, a core that carries flux with no loss and requires no magnetizing current, and perfect coupling, meaning every line of flux links every turn of both windings. Under these assumptions three simple laws hold exactly. The voltage law: the ratio of secondary to primary voltage equals the ratio of secondary to primary turns. A transformer with 230 turns on the primary and 23 on the secondary, connected to 230 volts, delivers 23 volts; the quantity volts per turn, here one volt per turn, is constant throughout the machine. The current law follows from conservation of energy: since an ideal transformer stores and dissipates nothing, output power equals input power, so volt-amperes in equal volt-amperes out, and current transforms inversely to voltage. Our ten-to-one step-down transformer delivering 10 amperes at 23 volts draws just 1 ampere at 230 volts. Step voltage down and current steps up in exact proportion, which is why the thick winding in a step-down transformer is the low-voltage one. The third law is subtler and enormously useful: impedance transformation. An impedance, the general form of resistance for alternating current, connected across the secondary appears from the primary side multiplied by the square of the turns ratio, because voltage scales by the ratio and current by its inverse, and impedance is their quotient. A loudspeaker of 8 ohms driven through a step-down transformer with a turns ratio of 25 to 1 looks to the amplifier like 8 times 625, or 5,000 ohms. This squaring is the basis of impedance matching, the practice of interposing a transformer so a source sees the load impedance at which it transfers power most effectively. Vacuum-tube audio amplifiers needed output transformers for exactly this reason, telephone lines used matching transformers called repeating coils, and radio-frequency circuits still use tiny transmission-line transformers, often on ratios like 4 to 1 or 9 to 1, to match antennas to feedlines. Worked example: a doorbell transformer steps 120 volts down to 16 volts to drive a chime drawing 1.2 amperes. Turns ratio: 120 divided by 16, which is 7.5 to 1. Primary current: 1.2 divided by 7.5, equal to 0.16 amperes. Power on both sides: about 19 watts. The chime's effective impedance of 13.3 ohms appears to the mains as 13.3 times 7.5 squared, roughly 750 ohms. Two practical notes complete the ideal picture. Winding polarity matters: the dots printed on schematic symbols mark terminals that swing positive together, and connecting windings in series aiding versus opposing adds or subtracts their voltages, which is how multi-tap and dual-voltage transformers offer 115 or 230 volt operation. And nothing in the ideal laws restricts direction: any transformer works backward as well as forward, stepping up where it once stepped down, a fact both useful in the laboratory and dangerous to forget around supposedly low-voltage windings.

sections.heading: Magnetic Cores: Materials, Flux, and Saturation
sections.body: The core is the transformer's silent partner, and its material physics sets most of the machine's limits. A core exists to give flux an easy path: magnetic materials are characterized by permeability, the measure of how much flux density a given magnetizing effort produces, and transformer steels have relative permeabilities in the thousands, meaning they conduct flux thousands of times more readily than air. Confining flux to a closed loop of such material ensures the same flux threads both windings, giving coupling coefficients above 0.99, and it reduces the magnetizing current to a few percent of rated current. The workhorse material for mains and grid transformers is silicon steel, iron alloyed with about three percent silicon, introduced by Robert Hadfield around 1900; the silicon raises the material's electrical resistivity, which suppresses the internal eddy currents discussed under losses, at the cost of making the steel harder and more brittle. A further refinement, cold-rolled grain-oriented steel developed by Norman Goss in the 1930s, aligns the metal's crystal grains along the rolling direction so the steel is magnetically easiest to use along the direction the flux actually travels; modern grain-oriented sheet is rolled to thicknesses of 0.23 to 0.35 millimeters, coated with insulating varnish, and stacked or wound into cores. Every magnetic material has a hard ceiling called saturation. Flux density, measured in teslas, cannot rise indefinitely: silicon steel saturates at roughly 1.8 to 2 teslas, and designers run cores at 1.5 to 1.7 teslas to leave margin. Beyond saturation the core behaves magnetically like air; incremental permeability collapses, the winding's inductance vanishes, and current, no longer restrained by back EMF, spikes to enormous peaks in narrow pulses each half cycle. A saturating transformer growls audibly, overheats quickly, and injects harmonic distortion into the supply. Saturation is why voltage and frequency ratings are inseparable: flux is proportional to applied voltage divided by frequency, so overvoltage or underfrequency both push the core toward the ceiling. Cores also remember: the relationship between magnetizing force and flux traces a loop called hysteresis rather than a single line, and material left magnetized at one point of the loop, remanence, is the root of the inrush phenomenon covered later in this guide. Core geometry matters nearly as much as material. The common shell-form core stamped from E and I shaped laminations surrounds the winding on both sides; core-form designs put windings on two legs of a rectangular loop; toroidal cores, continuous rings wound from steel strip, close the magnetic path with no joints at all, which cuts magnetizing current, stray field, and hum, at the price of expensive winding. Any joint or air gap in the path adds reluctance, the magnetic analogue of resistance, raising magnetizing current; manufacturers interleave lamination joints to minimize effective gaps. Deliberate gaps, useless in pure transformers, are added in inductors and flyback transformers precisely because a gap lets the core store energy without saturating.

sections.heading: Where the Energy Goes: Copper, Hysteresis, and Eddy Losses
sections.body: Real transformers waste power in two places, the windings and the core, and the taxonomy of these losses drives nearly every construction decision. Winding loss, universally called copper loss even when the conductor is aluminum, is ordinary resistive heating: current squared times winding resistance. It rises with the square of load, is zero at no load, and is attacked by using fatter conductors, shorter turns, and better filling of the available window with metal. At high frequencies two additional effects inflate the effective resistance. The skin effect crowds alternating current toward a conductor's surface, the characteristic depth being about 9.2 millimeters in copper at 50 hertz but only 0.66 millimeters at 10 kilohertz, so the interior of a thick wire carries little current. The proximity effect, often worse, is the crowding of current caused by the magnetic fields of neighboring turns. Designers answer with litz wire, bundles of many individually insulated fine strands woven so each strand samples all positions in the bundle, or with thin foil windings. Core loss, by contrast, depends on voltage and frequency but not on load, and it has two components. Hysteresis loss is the energy spent reversing the core's magnetic domains twice per cycle; it equals the area of the material's hysteresis loop times the frequency times core volume, and follows the empirical law published by Charles Steinmetz in 1892, rising roughly with frequency and with flux density to a power of about 1.6 to 2. Eddy-current loss arises because the core is itself a conductor bathed in changing flux; Faraday's law drives circulating currents within the steel, heating it uselessly. The remedy, laminating the core from thin sheets insulated from one another and oriented parallel to the flux, breaks the current loops; eddy loss falls with the square of lamination thickness, which is why sheets are rolled so thin and why higher-frequency cores abandon steel entirely for materials described later. Amorphous metal cores, glassy iron-boron alloys quenched so fast no crystals form, cut core loss to about a third of the best silicon steel and are increasingly used in distribution transformers, where the unit is energized around the clock and no-load loss dominates the lifetime energy bill. The load-dependence split has an elegant consequence for efficiency: a transformer's efficiency peaks at the load where copper loss equals core loss, and since distribution transformers idle much of the day, they are deliberately designed to peak at half load or below. Representative numbers make the scale concrete: a 100 volt-ampere wall transformer may be only 80 percent efficient; a 25 kilovolt-ampere pole transformer around 98.5 percent; a large grid transformer 99.5 to 99.85 percent. Even the last fraction matters at scale: transformer losses are estimated at two to three percent of all electricity generated worldwide, which is why efficiency standards such as the European Union's Ecodesign tiers and the United States Department of Energy rules keep tightening, and why utilities buy transformers on lifetime loss evaluation, paying thousands of dollars per kilowatt of rated loss avoided.

sections.heading: The Real Transformer: Equivalent Circuit, Regulation, and Efficiency
sections.body: Engineers tame the real transformer's imperfections by drawing it as an ideal transformer surrounded by a small collection of circuit elements, each standing for one physical defect; this equivalent circuit, standard since Steinmetz's era, lets ordinary circuit analysis predict everything measurable at the terminals. In series with the primary sits a resistance representing that winding's copper, and a small inductance called leakage reactance representing the fraction of flux that loops around the primary without ever reaching the secondary; the secondary gets a matching pair. In parallel across the input hang two more elements: a resistance whose dissipation equals the core loss, and the magnetizing inductance, which draws the current that keeps the core magnetized. For calculation, secondary elements are usually reflected to the primary side by multiplying by the turns ratio squared, collapsing the machine into one loop. Two cheap tests measure every parameter. The open-circuit test applies rated voltage with the secondary unloaded: the tiny input power is essentially pure core loss, and the input current is the magnetizing branch. The short-circuit test shorts the secondary and raises primary voltage until rated current flows, typically at only five to ten percent of rated voltage: at such low flux the core losses vanish, so the input power is essentially pure copper loss, and the voltage-to- current ratio gives the combined series impedance. That series impedance, expressed as the percent of rated voltage needed to drive rated current through the short, is stamped on every power transformer nameplate as percent impedance, typically four to ten percent, and it governs two opposed concerns: voltage regulation and fault current. Regulation is the droop of output voltage from no load to full load, caused by rated current flowing through the series resistance and leakage reactance; a transformer with five percent impedance serving a lagging power-factor load may droop three to four percent. Fault current is the mirror image: with a dead short on the secondary, current is limited only by that same impedance, so a five percent impedance unit delivers roughly twenty times rated current into a fault, which downstream breakers must interrupt. Designers choose impedance deliberately, low for stiff voltage, high to choke faults and to share load between paralleled units, which must match impedance to share fairly. Efficiency falls out of the same model: output power divided by output plus core loss plus load-squared-scaled copper loss. A worked example: a 50 kilovolt-ampere transformer with 200 watts core loss and 800 watts full-load copper loss is 98.06 percent efficient at full load at unity power factor, 98.55 percent at half load, where copper loss has fallen to a quarter, and its efficiency peaks precisely where the two losses are equal, at exactly half load in this instance, at 98.58 percent. The leakage reactance deserves a final word of respect: deliberately enlarged, it becomes a feature, providing the built-in current limiting of arc-welding transformers, neon-sign transformers, and microwave-oven transformers, all of which are designed leaky on purpose so their output current saturates safely at a chosen ceiling.

sections.heading: Construction: Windings, Insulation, and Cooling
sections.body: Turning electromagnetic theory into a durable machine is a problem of materials under stress, and transformer construction has evolved into a settled discipline. Windings are copper in most sizes, aluminum in many distribution units where its lower cost outweighs its bulk; small transformers use round enameled wire, larger ones rectangular strip or continuously transposed cable, and the highest current windings use foil. The two windings are almost never placed on separate legs as textbook diagrams suggest, because that would create huge leakage; instead they are wound concentrically, the low-voltage winding usually innermost around the core, the high-voltage winding over it, or in interleaved pancake sections for better coupling and controlled leakage. Every turn must be insulated from its neighbors, every layer from the next, every winding from the other and from the grounded core, and the insulation system, not the copper or steel, is what ages and dies: an old rule of thumb credited to Montsinger holds that each eight to ten degrees Celsius of extra operating temperature roughly halves insulation life. Insulation systems carry letter classes defining maximum hot-spot temperature, class A at 105 degrees Celsius, B at 130, F at 155, H at 180, and modern dry transformers commonly use class F or H materials such as Nomex aramid paper. Dry-type transformers, cooled by air, serve indoors up to a few megavolt-amperes, often with windings vacuum-cast in epoxy resin against moisture and dust. Larger and outdoor units are almost universally oil-immersed: the tank is filled with mineral oil, or increasingly with less flammable natural or synthetic esters, and the oil performs three jobs at once, insulating far better than air, carrying heat from windings to tank and radiators by convection, and, impregnating the kraft-paper wrap of the conductors to form the classic oil-paper dielectric. Cooling designations on nameplates encode the method in four letters: ONAN means oil natural, air natural, pure convection; ONAF adds fans on the radiators; OFAF pumps the oil; ODWF forces oil through directed ducts with water-cooled heat exchangers. Many grid transformers carry dual or triple ratings, perhaps 60 megavolt-amperes ONAN rising to 100 with fans and pumps running. Around the active parts cluster the accessories that keep the system healthy: porcelain or polymer bushings carry the conductors through the grounded tank wall; a conservator tank or a sealed nitrogen blanket accommodates the oil's thermal expansion; a silica-gel breather dries incoming air, because water is insulation's great enemy, with a few tens of parts per million of moisture in oil markedly lowering its breakdown strength; a Buchholz relay in the pipe to the conservator, invented in 1921, traps gas bubbles generated by internal arcing and trips the transformer before minor faults become explosions. Finally, most power transformers include tap changers, switches selecting among extra winding turns, typically plus or minus two and a half and five percent, to trim voltage; off-load tap changers require de-energization, while on-load tap changers step under full load and are the only routinely moving part in the machine.

sections.heading: Power Transformers and the Electric Grid
sections.body: The electric grid is, structurally, a cascade of transformers, and its voltage tiers exist because of them. Generation happens at moderate voltage, since slot insulation inside generators becomes impractical much beyond about 25 kilovolts. A generator step-up transformer immediately raises this to transmission level, 115 to 765 kilovolts depending on country and distance, with 400 kilovolts typical in Europe and 345 or 500 in much of North America; at these voltages a line can carry gigawatts with only a few percent loss over hundreds of kilometers. Transmission substations interconnect lines and step down to subtransmission levels around 66 to 138 kilovolts, distribution substations step down again to medium voltage, commonly 11 or 33 kilovolts in Europe-influenced systems and 12.47 to 34.5 kilovolts in North America, and finally millions of distribution transformers, on poles, on ground pads, or in vaults, make the last conversion to utilization voltage. There the architectures diverge interestingly: North America favors many small transformers, 10 to 100 kilovolt-amperes, each serving a handful of homes with a center-tapped 240 volt secondary whose midpoint ground yields the familiar split phase 120/240 service, while European practice uses fewer, larger units, 315 to 1000 kilovolt-amperes, each feeding hundreds of customers at 230/400 volts three-phase. Almost everything above the service drop is three-phase, and three-phase transformation adds a layer of topology: either a bank of three single-phase units or a single three-legged core, with each side's windings connected in one of two patterns, delta, a closed triangle, or wye, a star with a common neutral point. The choices are encoded in vector-group symbols like Dyn11, meaning delta primary, wye secondary with neutral brought out, and a thirty-degree phase shift with the secondary leading. Delta windings circulate the troublesome third-harmonic magnetizing currents harmlessly and need no neutral; wye windings provide the grounded neutral that distribution requires and halve the insulation stress per winding leg. The standard distribution unit is consequently Dyn: delta on the medium-voltage side, wye at the service. The thirty-degree shifts matter operationally, since transformers can only be paralleled if their vector groups and impedances agree, and deliberately opposed shifts are exploited to cancel harmonics in rectifier installations. Two grid-scale special cases complete the picture. Very large interties often use autotransformers, discussed later, for their economy when ratios are small. And high-voltage direct current converter stations bracket their electronics with converter transformers that are among the most stressed machines built, carrying combined alternating and direct voltage stress and heavy harmonic currents. At every level, the transformer is the grid's node of control as well as conversion: tap changers regulate feeder voltage, impedances set fault levels, and the loss evaluation of thousands of always-energized units is a permanent economic concern of every utility.

sections.heading: Instrument Transformers: Measuring Safely at Scale
sections.body: A wall of switchgear cannot put ten thousand amperes or four hundred thousand volts directly into a meter or a protective relay, so the grid runs on a specialized family of accurately scaled replicas produced by instrument transformers. A current transformer, or CT, is a transformer used inside out: the power conductor itself, passing once through a toroidal core, forms a one-turn primary, and a secondary of many turns delivers a proportional small current, standardized at 5 amperes, or 1 ampere in European practice, at rated primary current. A CT marked 600:5 delivers five amperes to the meters when six hundred amperes flow in the bus. Because the primary is the protected circuit itself, the CT's burden, the impedance of the meters and wiring it feeds, must stay low, and its accuracy is specified in classes such as 0.3 for revenue metering or C400 for protection, the latter guaranteeing usable accuracy at twenty times rated current so relays can still see faults faithfully. One property of CTs is infamous and lethal enough to repeat everywhere: the secondary must never be open-circuited while the primary carries current. In normal operation the secondary's counter-magnetomotive force cancels almost all of the primary's; break the secondary loop and that cancellation vanishes, the core drives into saturation on every half cycle, and the many-turn winding develops kilovolt spikes that can flash over, destroy the CT, and kill. CT secondaries are therefore shorted at a dedicated shorting block before any meter is disconnected.
