A negative cloud-to-ground stroke delivers a median current around 30 kiloamperes, with severe strokes exceeding 100 and the standards designing for 200; the current rises in a microsecond or two, and its energy will find a path to earth through whatever presents itself, masonry, roof timbers, telephone wiring, or a person in a doorway. The discipline of lightning protection, codified in IEC 62305 internationally and NFPA 780 in the United States, is the art of offering it a better path and managing the consequences of that much current flowing through it.

The external system descends from Benjamin Franklin's rod of 1752 with refinements of geometry rather than principle. Air terminals, rods or a mesh of conductors on the roof, are placed using the rolling sphere method: imagine a sphere of radius 20 to 60 meters, depending on protection level, rolled over the structure; anywhere it touches is a candidate strike point and must carry a terminal. Down conductors, at least two on any structure and spaced around it, carry the current to earth by the straightest possible routes, because at lightning frequencies inductance dominates resistance; a bend of small radius presents enough impedance that the stroke may sidefash, arcing across air to a better path, which is why sharp bends and re-entrant loops are forbidden. Each down conductor terminates in the earth termination, ideally a ring electrode around the building tied to the foundation electrode, presenting low impedance and controlling the surface gradient so that step voltage near the walls stays survivable.

Bonding at the lightning scale becomes non-negotiable. IEC 62305 requires every metallic service entering the structure to be bonded to the lightning earth at the entry point, directly for pipes, through surge protective devices for live conductors, because a stroke raising the building earth by hundreds of kilovolts relative to remote earth would otherwise drive that difference across the insulation of every appliance connected to the incoming cables. Isolated masts and overhead shield wires protect explosive stores and tank farms by keeping the stroke current away from the structure entirely, at the cost of careful separation distances calculated so the mast cannot flash over to what it guards.

Surge protection extends the defense from the direct stroke to the far commoner induced and conducted transients, including those from strokes kilometers away and from utility switching. Surge protective devices are staged: Type 1 units at the service, built on spark gaps or heavy metal-oxide varistors, divert the large fraction of a direct-stroke current; Type 2 units at distribution boards clamp the residue; Type 3 units at sensitive equipment trim the last hundreds of volts. Their ratings, given as nominal and maximum discharge currents with 8/20 microsecond test waves for Types 2 and 3 and 10/350 waves for Type 1, only mean anything when the device has a short, straight, low-inductance connection to the earthing system; a surge arrester on 3 meters of coiled wire is largely decorative, since each meter of conductor adds on the order of a microhenry, and a 10-kiloampere-per-microsecond rise across it develops kilovolts. The earthing electrode, the bonding network and the arresters are therefore one system, and the recurring theme of this guide holds at its most dramatic here: the performance is set not by any single component but by the geometry of the whole loop.

sections.heading: Signal Grounding, Ground Loops and Noise in Electronics
sections.body:
The word ground does a second job in electronics: it names the reference conductor against which signals are measured, and the collision between this meaning and safety earthing produces the most commonly encountered grounding problem in ordinary life, the ground loop. The classic symptom is a steady hum, at 50 or 60 hertz or their low harmonics, from an audio system the moment two pieces of mains-powered equipment are connected by a signal cable, or slanting bars crawling through an analog video picture. Nothing is faulty in the safety sense; the system is doing exactly what its topology dictates.

The mechanism is worth seeing clearly. Each device's chassis and signal reference are tied, for safety, to the protective earth of its own outlet. The signal cable's shield now joins the two chassis, closing a conductive loop: shield, chassis A, earth wiring back to the panel, earth wiring out to chassis B, shield again. Two things drive current around such a loop. Small voltage differences, millivolts to volts, exist between the earth terminals of different outlets because of return currents and shared impedances in the building wiring; connected by the low-resistance shield, those millivolts drive appreciable current along it, and the resulting voltage drop along the shield resistance adds directly into the signal on an unbalanced connection. Second, the loop is a one-turn transformer secondary threading whatever stray magnetic flux the building's wiring and transformers produce, inducing current at the mains frequency. The loop area, not any component, sets the coupling, which is why rerouting cables sometimes cures what replacing equipment did not.

The legitimate cures are the ones that break the loop for signals while preserving it for safety. Balanced interconnections, standard in professional audio through XLR connectors and in Ethernet through its transformers, transmit the signal as a difference between two conductors and reject whatever voltage the shield carries, tolerating tens of volts of ground difference. Isolation transformers in the signal path, optical links such as TOSLINK, and the optocouplers and digital isolators inside industrial interfaces pass information across an insulation barrier with no conductive loop at all. For measurement systems, the discipline of single-point or star grounding, running each subsystem's reference separately to one node rather than daisy-chaining, keeps heavy return currents out of sensitive references at low frequencies, while at radio frequencies the opposite doctrine rules, a multipoint bond to a continuous plane, because at those frequencies conductor inductance makes long star spokes useless and the plane's low impedance wins; mixed-signal design is largely the negotiation between these two regimes. Shield connection follows the same frequency split, and the long argument about grounding a cable shield at one end or both resolves into practice: one end favored for low-frequency analog runs to stop shield current, both ends for RF and digital, sometimes with a capacitor at one end to satisfy both masters.

The illegitimate cure demands naming because it recurs in every generation of forum advice: lifting the safety earth with a two-prong cheater adapter or by snapping the pin. It often silences the hum, by opening the loop, and it converts the chassis into a trap that waits for the first internal fault to become live at line voltage. Hum is an annoyance; a floating faulted chassis is a fatality mechanism. Every reputable audio engineering reference, and the codes themselves, put this beyond debate: the safety ground is never the adjustment point.

sections.heading: Static Electricity and Earthing in Hazardous and Sensitive Places
sections.body:
The third family of earthing practice deals with charges measured in microamperes and millijoules rather than kiloamperes, and it matters at both ends of a strange scale: energies too small for a person to feel can destroy semiconductor devices, and sparks a person barely notices can ignite vapors and dust clouds. Static electricity accumulates whenever dissimilar materials contact and separate, the triboelectric effect; a person walking across synthetic carpet in dry air can reach 15,000 to 35,000 volts, and even walking on a vinyl floor at higher humidity leaves hundreds to thousands of volts on the body. The stored energy is tiny, but the discharge is fast, and its consequences depend entirely on what receives it.

Modern electronics receives it badly. Gate oxides in integrated circuits are damaged by discharges of a few hundred volts, and some sensitive components by tens of volts, far below the roughly 3,000-volt threshold at which a person feels a spark at all, so most electrostatic damage is invisible to the person causing it and appears later as unexplained failure. The electronics industry's response, codified in the standard ANSI/ESD S20.20 and its IEC 61340 counterparts, is an earthing system in miniature called the electrostatic protected area. Work surfaces are dissipative, not conductive, with surface resistances in the megohm to gigohm range, and drain to a common point; personnel wear wrist straps whose cords contain a series resistor of one megohm, large enough to limit current to a safe trickle if the wearer contacts mains voltage, small enough to bleed body charge in milliseconds; floors, footwear, garments and chairs are specified and audited, and ionizers neutralize charge on the insulators that cannot be grounded at all, such as plastic packaging. The through-line is the same equipotential logic as building bonding: damage needs a voltage difference, and the system denies differences by connecting everything, slowly, through resistance.

Where flammable atmospheres exist, the stakes change from hardware to lives. A spark of about 0.2 to 0.3 millijoules ignites gasoline vapor and many solvent vapors; hydrogen ignites at under 0.02 millijoules; suspended dusts of grain, sugar, aluminum and flour ignite in the low tens of millijoules, and dust explosions have leveled elevators and mills, from the Washburn A Mill disaster in Minneapolis in 1878 to the Imperial Sugar refinery explosion in Georgia in 2008. A human body at a few kilovolts stores on the order of a dozen millijoules, comfortably above several of those thresholds. Industry standards, NFPA 77 on static electricity and API RP 2003 for petroleum operations, therefore require bonding and grounding wherever flammable liquids and powders move: the tank truck is bonded to the loading rack before hoses connect; drums and receiving vessels are bonded together during transfer so no potential difference can spark across the falling liquid stream; flow rates are limited and splash filling avoided because the flow itself generates the charge; operators wear dissipative footwear on conductive floors. The dramatic small-scale example is the fire at the fuel pump, a documented pattern in which a driver re-enters the car during filling, recharges by sliding across the seat, and sparks to the nozzle; the counter-measure is the habit of touching the vehicle body away from the filler before touching the nozzle, a one-gesture equipotential bond. Across all these settings the physics never changes, only the budget: keep connected what must agree, drain what accumulates, and never let a difference wait where energy or vapor can meet it.

sections.heading: Common Faults, Testing and What Home Wiring Actually Does
sections.body:
The earthing defects found in real buildings form a short and repetitive list, which is good news, because it means a methodical check finds most of them. The commonest is the open ground: a receptacle whose earth terminal connects to nothing, through a broken conductor, a never-connected wire in a renovation, or an ungrounded two-wire circuit fitted with three-slot outlets. Next is reversed polarity, line and neutral swapped, which leaves lamp shells and appliance internals live when switched off. Then the bootleg ground described earlier, neutral jumpered to earth at the outlet, which fools simple testers and energizes cases through the neutral's voltage drop; its high-resistance cousin, earth continuity present but poor, shows up only under measurement. In the panel and around the building the recurring finds are neutral-to-earth bonds added downstream of the main bonding point, corroded or painted-over electrode clamps, grounding conductors severed by landscaping or plumbing work, bonding jumpers removed when a water meter or section of metal pipe was replaced with plastic and never reinstated, and in older stock, entire installations relying on a gas or water pipe earth that plastic renewals have quietly disconnected street-side.

A sensible layered approach to checking exists for a careful lay person, with a firm boundary where professional work begins. The first layer is the plug-in receptacle tester, a few dollars, whose lamp codes reveal open ground, open neutral and reversals in seconds per outlet; versions with a ground fault test button also exercise GFCI protection. Understand its limits: it cannot detect a bootleg ground or quantify a marginal one. The second layer is exercising every RCD, GFCI and AFCI by its test button monthly, and noting any device that will not trip or will not reset. The third layer is observation: tingles from any appliance or plumbing fixture, hum that appears when equipment is interconnected, breakers or RCDs that trip in rain, scorch marks or warmth at outlets, and any clamp or green wire found disconnected during other work; each of these is a finding to report, not a curiosity. Everything beyond, loop impedance measurement at the sockets, insulation resistance testing, earth electrode measurement by fall of potential or clamp, verification of bonding milliohm values, and all repairs inside panels, is instrumented, partly live work for a licensed electrician, and in many jurisdictions legally so. Periodic formal inspection is codified in some countries, such as the British electrical installation condition report on a cycle of five to ten years for dwellings, and buying an older property is everywhere the natural trigger for one.

It helps, finally, to hold the historical picture, because the housing stock is a geological record of code eras. Equipment grounding conductors to general-purpose receptacles became mandatory in North America in the early 1960s, so mid-century houses often have original two-wire circuits; GFCI requirements arrived with the 1971 NEC for outdoor and pool receptacles and spread edition by edition to bathrooms in 1975, kitchens in 1987, and most damp or accessible locations since; AFCI requirements began with bedrooms in 1999 and broadened after. Where an old two-wire circuit survives, modern codes typically allow three practical remedies: rewire with a grounding circuit, fit a GFCI and label the outlets no equipment ground, which protects people though it cannot ground a surge protector, or leave two-slot receptacles in place. What the codes never allow is the pretense of safety, a grounding-type receptacle on a circuit that cannot ground it, and that principle, no pretense, is a fair one-sentence summary of the whole discipline this guide has described.

guides.safetyNote: Mains electricity can injure or kill, and grounding faults are especially dangerous because a system can appear to work normally while the protection is missing. Never open a service panel, disconnect a grounding or bonding conductor, or work on fixed wiring unless you are qualified and the circuit is proven dead with a tested voltage indicator; an interrupted earth conductor can rise to full line voltage the moment a fault occurs elsewhere. Testing earth electrodes and fault loop impedance involves live measurements that belong to trained people with proper instruments. In most places, work on the grounding electrode system, the main bonding, or the service equipment is regulated and must be done or inspected by a licensed electrician. When in doubt, test with a plug-in tester, note the fault, and hire a professional rather than improvising.
